laws.title: Taliban Governance and the IEA
laws.subtitle: Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan — Post-2021
laws.fullDescription: Since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021 — following the US military withdrawal — Afghanistan is governed as the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA). The Taliban have suspended the 2004 constitution and govern through a Supreme Leader (Haibatullah Akhundzada, based in Kandahar) and ministerial structure. No country formally recognizes the IEA government. The Taliban's governance applies a strict interpretation of Sharia law — eliminating most fundamental rights recognized by international standards. Women have been largely excluded from public life, government, and education.
laws.penalty: Opposition to IEA rule: execution or long imprisonment; criticizing Taliban leadership: arrest and torture; unauthorized political organizing: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Diplomats and international organizations in Afghanistan operate under negotiated access frameworks
Tribal jirga (council) decisions may in some areas operate alongside formal Taliban governance

quiz.q: Who is the Taliban's Supreme Leader governing Afghanistan?
options: Mullah Omar (deceased)
Ashraf Ghani
Haibatullah Akhundzada — based in Kandahar
Sirajuddin Haqqani
quiz.explanation: Haibatullah Akhundzada is the Taliban's Supreme Leader (Amir al-Mu'minin) since 2016, governing Afghanistan from Kandahar following the Taliban's return to power in August 2021. He is the highest religious and political authority in the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, issuing decrees on all major governance matters including women's rights restrictions, though he rarely appears in public.

laws.title: Women's Rights Under Taliban
laws.subtitle: Gender Apartheid — Education, Employment, Public Space
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's return has resulted in what UN experts call 'gender apartheid' — systematic elimination of women's rights. Key restrictions: girls banned from secondary school and university (since 2021 and 2022 respectively); women banned from most government employment; banned from parks, gyms, and public spaces without male guardian (mahram); banned from NGO and UN local employment (2022); women's faces must be covered in public. These policies have been condemned by virtually every country and international organization. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to ban girls' education.
laws.penalty: Women appearing in public without mahram: arrest of woman and male relatives; girls attending secondary school: closure of school and arrest of teachers; women working in banned roles: employer sanctions and arrest
exceptions: Women may work in healthcare — though restrictions have tightened
Sharia-compliant education for girls (Quranic studies) continues in some areas

quiz.q: What makes Afghanistan unique globally regarding girls' education?
options: Afghanistan has the world's highest female literacy rate
Afghanistan is the only country in the world to ban girls from secondary and university education
Afghanistan requires girls to attend religious-only schools
Afghanistan has achieved universal primary education for girls
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan under Taliban rule is the only country in the world to have banned girls from attending secondary school and university. Since 2021, girls above sixth grade have been prohibited from attending school; since 2022, women have been banned from universities. UN experts have classified this as 'gender apartheid' — systematic elimination of women from public and educational life.

laws.title: Frozen Assets and Economic Collapse
laws.subtitle: USD 9.5 Billion Afghan Central Bank Reserves
laws.fullDescription: After the Taliban takeover, the US froze approximately USD 9.5 billion in Afghan central bank reserves held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. These reserves — Afghanistan's entire sovereign savings — remain largely frozen. Half was directed to a Swiss trust (AFIAT) for humanitarian use, subject to conditions the Taliban have not met. The Afghan economy collapsed — the currency plummeted, imports of basic goods became difficult, and poverty reached catastrophic levels. International aid — prohibited from flowing through Taliban government — is channeled through NGOs and UN agencies, providing a lifeline but not replacing government function.
laws.penalty: Sanctions violation — dealing with Taliban-designated individuals or entities: criminal prosecution in sanctioning countries; unauthorized access to frozen Afghan assets: US/EU sanctions prosecution
exceptions: Humanitarian aid transactions exempted from sanctions under OFAC (US) and EU humanitarian exceptions
Informal hawala money transfer networks continue with modified compliance requirements

quiz.q: Where are Afghanistan's frozen central bank reserves held?
options: In Kabul at Da Afghanistan Bank
In Swiss banks
Approximately USD 9.5 billion at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — frozen after the Taliban takeover
In Saudi Arabia under GCC custodianship
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's approximately USD 9.5 billion in central bank reserves are held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — frozen by the US government after the Taliban's return in August 2021. Half was subsequently placed in a Swiss-based trust (AFIAT) intended for humanitarian use. These reserves represent Afghanistan's entire sovereign savings and their freeze has contributed significantly to economic collapse.

laws.title: Taliban Justice System
laws.subtitle: Sharia Courts and Hudud Punishments
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have replaced Afghanistan's previous court system with Sharia courts applying the Taliban's strict interpretation of Islamic criminal law. Hudud punishments — those specified in Islamic jurisprudence for specific crimes — include: amputation for theft, flogging for alcohol consumption and fornication, and stoning for adultery. The Taliban have publicly conducted executions and amputations in Kabul's sports stadium. Trials are summary — with little due process, no legal representation, and torture documented in detention. The UN and human rights organizations document systematic judicial torture.
laws.penalty: Theft: hand amputation (Taliban hudud application); adultery: death by stoning; murder: death penalty or blood money (diya); alcohol consumption: flogging; fornication: flogging
exceptions: Blood money (diya) payment to victim's family may prevent execution in murder cases
Juvenile offenders subject to modified sentences though enforcement is inconsistent

quiz.q: What types of punishments have the Taliban reinstated in Afghanistan's justice system?
options: Only fines and imprisonment
Hudud punishments including amputation for theft, flogging for alcohol, and stoning for adultery
Community service and rehabilitation
Only death penalty for the most serious crimes
quiz.explanation: The Taliban have reinstated hudud punishments from their strict Sharia interpretation — including amputation of hands for theft, flogging for alcohol consumption and fornication, and stoning for adultery. Public executions and amputations have been carried out in sports stadiums. UN documentation confirms these punishments are applied with minimal due process and torture in detention is widespread.

laws.title: Humanitarian Crisis
laws.subtitle: World's Largest Humanitarian Emergency
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan is host to one of the world's largest humanitarian crises. Over 28 million Afghans (two-thirds of the population) need humanitarian assistance. Severe acute malnutrition threatens millions of children. Healthcare system has partially collapsed — medical personnel (especially female doctors) have fled or been removed. UN agencies (WFP, UNICEF, OCHA, WHO) and NGOs provide critical services. Donor fatigue is reducing funding. The Taliban's ban on female NGO and UN workers (2022) has severely limited humanitarian access — particularly to women and girls who refuse to be served by male aid workers.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of UN/NGO aid delivery: violations handled through diplomatic and humanitarian pressure — no formal enforcement mechanism in IEA
exceptions: Healthcare workers may operate in some areas with special Taliban authorization — particularly male medical workers
Emergency food distribution may reach communities through local networks bypassing Taliban restrictions in some cases

quiz.q: How many Afghans need humanitarian assistance?
options: About 5 million
Around 10 million
Over 28 million — two-thirds of the population
The entire population of 40 million
quiz.explanation: Over 28 million Afghans — approximately two-thirds of the country's population — require humanitarian assistance. This extraordinary figure reflects the compound crises facing Afghanistan: economic collapse following the Taliban takeover, frozen international aid, severe drought, decades of conflict, destroyed infrastructure, and the systematic dismantling of education and health systems. It is one of the largest humanitarian emergencies in the world.

laws.title: Water Crisis and Drought
laws.subtitle: Climate Change and Agricultural Collapse
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan faces a severe water crisis — driven by climate change (reduced snowpack in the Hindu Kush mountains), drought, and destroyed irrigation infrastructure from decades of war. The Amu Darya (Oxus) river — shared with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan — is a critical transboundary resource. The Kajaki and Arghandab dams need repair. Over 80% of Afghans depend on agriculture, making drought catastrophic for food security. The Helmand River basin (Afghanistan-Iran) is a source of diplomatic tension over water allocation. Climate change is increasing drought frequency and severity.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: water theft from irrigation systems: community-based dispute resolution; dam sabotage: severe criminal penalties
exceptions: Emergency water access during severe drought has informal community distribution norms recognized by Taliban authorities
International humanitarian water supply programs operate under OCHA coordination exemptions

quiz.q: What percentage of Afghans depend on agriculture — making drought particularly devastating?
options: About 20%
Around 40%
Over 80%
Only a few percent — most Afghans live in cities
quiz.explanation: Over 80% of Afghanistan's population depends on agriculture for their livelihoods — making the combination of drought, climate change, and war-destroyed irrigation infrastructure catastrophic for food security. When crops fail, the majority of Afghans have no alternative income. Afghanistan's agricultural collapse is a primary driver of the humanitarian emergency.

laws.title: Press Freedom and Media Suppression
laws.subtitle: Reporters Without Borders — World's Worst
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's media — which had developed significantly between 2001-2021 — has been largely destroyed under Taliban rule. Independent TV stations, newspapers, and radio outlets have closed or been brought under Taliban control. Female journalists have been barred from broadcasting. Taliban decree bans women from appearing on TV or in entertainment programs. Over 200 media outlets closed in the first year of Taliban rule; over 80% of journalists lost jobs. Afghanistan ranks last or near-last globally on press freedom indices. Foreign journalists face significant danger. Self-censorship is universal.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized journalism: detention, torture, and execution documented; publishing anti-Taliban content: arrest and imprisonment; photographing Taliban fighters without permission: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Foreign journalists with Taliban media accreditation have limited operating space — though arbitrary detention continues
State media (RTA) journalists operate under direct Taliban direction

quiz.q: How many Afghan media outlets closed in the first year of Taliban rule?
options: About 10
Around 50
Over 200 — with 80%+ of journalists losing their jobs
All media closed immediately
quiz.explanation: Over 200 Afghan media outlets closed in the first year following the Taliban's August 2021 return — more than 80% of journalists lost their jobs. Female journalists were barred from broadcasting, independent TV stations closed or were brought under Taliban control, and self-censorship became universal. Afghanistan's vibrant media sector, built over 20 years of international support, was effectively destroyed within months.

laws.title: Opium Economy and Drug Trade
laws.subtitle: Taliban Drug Ban and Poppy Eradication
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has long produced 80-90% of the world's opium — the heroin supply chain. In April 2022, Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah issued a decree banning opium poppy cultivation. Eradication campaigns have dramatically reduced cultivation — with major declines in 2023 UNODC estimates. However, the ban has devastated the livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers who depend on poppy income. Alternative development programs struggle to replace poppy income. The Taliban's ability to enforce the ban varies by region. The Taliban themselves derived significant revenue from taxing the drug trade before taking power.
laws.penalty: Opium poppy cultivation: crop destruction and imprisonment; drug trafficking: execution (Taliban policy for major traffickers); drug use: flogging and imprisonment
exceptions: Taliban decree does not explicitly address existing opium stocks — trade in stockpiled product continues legally ambiguous
Medical morphine precursor cultivation under strict authorization — though practically suspended

quiz.q: What share of global opium production did Afghanistan historically account for?
options: About 20%
Around 50%
80-90% of the world's opium — virtually the entire global supply chain
Only a small fraction — Colombia is the main source
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan historically produced 80-90% of the world's opium — making it virtually the sole source of global heroin supply. The Taliban's 2022 ban on poppy cultivation, while dramatically reducing cultivation, has devastated the livelihoods of millions of Afghan farmers who had no viable alternative cash crop, contributing to the humanitarian crisis.

laws.title: Human Rights Abuses — UN Documentation
laws.subtitle: UNAMA Reports and Enforced Disappearances
laws.fullDescription: The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) has documented systematic human rights abuses under Taliban rule: extrajudicial killings of former government officials and Afghan security forces; torture in detention; enforced disappearances; collective punishment of communities sheltering resistance fighters; and restrictions on freedom of movement and expression. UNAMA's access to monitor abuses has been severely constrained. The International Criminal Court has jurisdiction and is investigating potential war crimes. Multiple former resistance commanders and government officials have been executed despite Taliban amnesty promises.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: no formal accountability for Taliban human rights abuses; individuals reporting abuses to UN: risk of arrest and torture
exceptions: Taliban have in some cases disciplined fighters for unauthorized killings — but accountability is minimal
International pressure has in isolated cases led to release of detained civil society members

quiz.q: What human rights documentation has UNAMA provided about Taliban rule?
options: UNAMA found no human rights violations
UNAMA documented extrajudicial killings, torture, enforced disappearances, and collective punishment
UNAMA praised Taliban governance improvements
UNAMA has been banned from Afghanistan entirely
quiz.explanation: UNAMA has documented systematic human rights abuses including extrajudicial killings of former officials, torture in Taliban detention, enforced disappearances, and collective punishment of communities. These violations continue despite Taliban promises of amnesty during the August 2021 transition. UNAMA's access is severely restricted, meaning documented cases likely represent a fraction of actual abuses.

laws.title: Education Collapse
laws.subtitle: Girls' Education Ban and Brain Drain
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's education system has largely collapsed under Taliban rule. Girls are banned from secondary school (since August 2021) and university (since December 2022). Boys' education continues but faces severe resource constraints. An estimated 3.7 million children are out of school — the vast majority are girls. Teachers — particularly female teachers — have fled or been unemployed. UNICEF and NGOs run informal education programs for girls in some areas. Afghanistan's educated professionals (doctors, engineers, teachers) have fled in massive numbers — creating a brain drain that will affect the country for generations.
laws.penalty: Operating girls' school above 6th grade: school closure and potential arrest of operators; educating girls in unauthorized settings: arrest risk; boys attending non-Taliban-approved schools: administrative closure
exceptions: Some areas (particularly northern Afghanistan) have maintained limited girls' education through local Taliban commander tolerance
Home-based tutoring — technically prohibited but enforcement varies by area

quiz.q: How many children are out of school in Afghanistan?
options: About 500,000
Around 1 million
Approximately 3.7 million — the vast majority girls
Only 100,000 in conflict-affected areas
quiz.explanation: Approximately 3.7 million children are out of school in Afghanistan — the vast majority of them girls excluded by the Taliban's education bans. This catastrophic education collapse, combined with massive brain drain as educated Afghans fled, threatens Afghanistan's human development for a generation. UN agencies and NGOs run informal educational programs but cannot reach all affected children.

laws.title: Reconstruction and Infrastructure
laws.subtitle: From 20 Years of Aid to Collapse
laws.fullDescription: Between 2001 and 2021, the US alone spent over USD 145 billion on Afghan reconstruction — the largest reconstruction effort in history. Roads, airports, electricity, schools, and healthcare facilities were built. Much of this infrastructure is now deteriorating without maintenance funding or staff. Power supply has collapsed in some cities — the Kajaki dam hydropower station needs repair. The US-trained Afghan army of 300,000 dissolved in days when the Taliban returned. International Monetary Fund, World Bank, and Asian Development Bank projects have been suspended. Afghan reconstruction now depends primarily on private remittances and UN aid.
laws.penalty: Destruction of public infrastructure: harsh Taliban punishment; theft from reconstruction projects: severe punishment under Taliban law
exceptions: Emergency infrastructure repair funded by UN humanitarian programs exempt from sanctions in some cases
Taliban allow some infrastructure maintenance by international contractors under negotiated access
laws.sourceLabel: SIGAR — Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction

quiz.q: How much did the US spend on Afghan reconstruction between 2001-2021?
options: About USD 10 billion
Around USD 50 billion
Over USD 145 billion — the largest reconstruction effort in history
USD 300 billion
quiz.explanation: The US spent over USD 145 billion on Afghan reconstruction between 2001 and 2021 — the largest reconstruction effort in American history. SIGAR (Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction) documented widespread waste, fraud, and abuse in this spending. Despite the investment, the Afghan government and security forces collapsed within days of US withdrawal, calling into question the entire reconstruction approach.

laws.title: Deforestation and Land Degradation
laws.subtitle: Pistachio Forests and Environmental Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has lost over 70% of its pistachio forests — once extensive in Badghis, Faryab, and other provinces. Deforestation from timber smuggling, fuel wood collection, and agricultural expansion has stripped mountainsides. Land degradation from decades of war (bombing, land mines, displacement), drought, and mismanagement has severely reduced agricultural productivity. Afghanistan has very limited environmental governance capacity. The Taliban have banned unauthorized logging in some areas — though enforcement is minimal. Climate change is accelerating desertification in southern and western Afghanistan.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: unauthorized logging: fines and potential corporal punishment; land mining causing environmental damage: informal community dispute resolution
exceptions: Fuel wood collection for household heating — practically tolerated given lack of alternatives
Emergency agricultural land clearing for survival farming recognized by Taliban authorities

quiz.q: How much of Afghanistan's pistachio forests have been lost?
options: About 10%
Around 30%
Over 70% of pistachio forests
Pistachio forests are still fully intact
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan has lost over 70% of its once-extensive pistachio forests — a devastating environmental and economic loss. These forests were not only ecologically important but provided livelihoods for millions of rural Afghans who harvested wild pistachios. Deforestation has been driven by timber smuggling, fuel wood collection, agricultural expansion, and decades of war and governance failure.

laws.title: International Isolation
laws.subtitle: No Country Recognizes the Taliban Government
laws.fullDescription: No country in the world has formally recognized the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA). Even Pakistan and China — countries with significant engagement — have not granted formal recognition. The UN seat is still held by the previous government's ambassador. Recognition is conditioned by most countries on girls' education, women's rights, and counter-terrorism commitments (particularly against al-Qaeda). The Taliban have not met any of these conditions. This creates a diplomatic limbo — countries must engage with Taliban-controlled institutions for aid delivery while refusing to recognize their legitimacy.
laws.penalty: Formal recognition of IEA would have no domestic legal penalty — but political cost to recognizing states would be severe international backlash
exceptions: Practical engagement for humanitarian purposes is distinguished from formal diplomatic recognition
UN 'credentials committee' has not resolved the contested Afghan seat — continuing the previous government's representation

quiz.q: Has any country formally recognized the Taliban's Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan?
options: Yes — Pakistan and China have recognized it
Yes — several Muslim-majority countries have recognized it
No — no country has formally recognized the IEA despite significant engagement
Yes — the UN has recognized it through the Security Council
quiz.explanation: No country has formally recognized the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA) — not even Pakistan, China, or other countries with significant engagement or interest in Afghan stability. Recognition has been conditioned on girls' education, women's rights, inclusive governance, and counter-terrorism commitments. The Taliban have met none of these conditions, maintaining Afghanistan's complete diplomatic isolation.

laws.title: Drug Law and Narcotics
laws.subtitle: Taliban Anti-Drug Policies and Enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's drug situation has dramatically shifted under Taliban rule. The Taliban's April 2022 decree banning opium cultivation was enforced through crop eradication — with UNODC estimating cultivation dropped by 95% in 2023. However, methamphetamine production (using locally growing ephedra plants) has increased — Afghanistan has become a significant meth producer. Drug trafficking routes through Central Asia to Russia and Europe continue with stockpiled opium. The Taliban's previous revenue from taxing the drug trade creates enforcement credibility challenges.
laws.penalty: Opium cultivation: crop destruction and imprisonment; drug trafficking (major): execution; drug use: flogging and forced treatment; methamphetamine production: similar severe penalties
exceptions: Traditional medicinal use of cannabis in some Afghan communities has informal recognition
Stockpiled opium from pre-2022 crops — legal status ambiguous during ban implementation

quiz.q: What drug has partially replaced opium production in Afghanistan under Taliban rule?
options: Heroin from other sources
Cocaine imports
Methamphetamine — using locally growing ephedra plants
Cannabis exclusively
quiz.explanation: While opium cultivation has dramatically dropped under Taliban bans, methamphetamine production has increased in Afghanistan — using locally growing ephedra plants (which naturally contain methamphetamine precursors). Afghanistan has become a significant methamphetamine producer and exporter, particularly to markets in Central Asia, South Asia, and the Middle East.

laws.title: Afghan Refugees and Displacement
laws.subtitle: 5+ Million Refugees and IDPs
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has one of the world's largest displaced populations. Over 5 million Afghans are refugees abroad — primarily in Pakistan and Iran — with the largest single refugee flows following the August 2021 Taliban takeover. Internally, 3+ million Afghans are IDPs. Pakistan has forced deportations of undocumented Afghans (2023 mass deportation campaign). Iran similarly deports Afghan workers. Western countries took over 200,000 Afghans in 2021 emergency evacuations. Afghan diaspora communities across Europe, North America, and Australia maintain significant ties. UNHCR coordinates refugee protection.
laws.penalty: Under host countries: unauthorized presence: deportation; under Taliban: returning refugees must comply with all Taliban rules or face prosecution
exceptions: UNHCR recognized refugees have non-refoulement protection under 1951 Refugee Convention
Afghan refugees with Western country permanent residency or citizenship have legal status in host countries

quiz.q: Where are the majority of Afghan refugees located?
options: Primarily in Europe and North America
In China and Russia
Primarily in Pakistan and Iran
Spread equally across all neighboring countries
quiz.explanation: The vast majority of Afghanistan's 5+ million refugees are in neighboring countries — primarily Pakistan (2.4+ million) and Iran (3+ million, including undocumented workers). The 2021 Taliban takeover generated a new wave of refugees, including the emergency evacuation of 200,000+ Afghans to Western countries. Pakistan and Iran have periodically conducted mass deportations under 'undocumented migrant' policies.

laws.title: Mineral Wealth and Chinese Investment
laws.subtitle: USD 3 Trillion in Untapped Minerals
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan sits on an estimated USD 3 trillion+ in untapped mineral resources — including copper (Mes Aynak, world's second-largest deposit), iron ore, lithium (significant deposits relevant to battery technology), rare earth elements, gold, and precious stones (lapis lazuli, emeralds). Previous attempts to develop these resources were blocked by insecurity and corruption. The Taliban have signaled openness to Chinese mining investment — CITIC signed a previous copper deal at Mes Aynak that has yet to be developed. Chinese companies are exploring lithium and copper opportunities. Mineral development remains largely stalled.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: unauthorized mining: severe criminal punishment; mineral smuggling: death penalty in some cases; foreign mining without Taliban authorization: confiscation and expulsion
exceptions: Artisanal small-scale gemstone mining (lapis lazuli, emeralds) — traditional livelihood with Taliban tax collection rather than prohibition
Emergency humanitarian program funding may include limited resource development components
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Mines and Petroleum Afghanistan

quiz.q: What is the estimated value of Afghanistan's untapped mineral resources?
options: About USD 100 million
Around USD 10 billion
Over USD 3 trillion — including copper, lithium, and rare earths
Afghanistan has no significant mineral resources
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's untapped mineral resources are estimated at over USD 3 trillion — including one of the world's largest copper deposits (Mes Aynak), significant lithium (critical for batteries), rare earth elements, iron ore, gold, and precious stones. This extraordinary mineral wealth has attracted Chinese interest — but insecurity, corruption, and infrastructure gaps have prevented large-scale development for decades.

laws.title: Taliban vs. ISIS-K Conflict
laws.subtitle: ISKP Terrorism and Taliban Counter-Terrorism
laws.fullDescription: Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP or ISIS-K) — the Afghan affiliate of ISIS — is in direct violent conflict with the Taliban, viewing them as insufficiently extreme. ISKP has conducted devastating attacks in Afghanistan including the August 2021 Kabul airport bombing (killing 183 people), Shia mosque bombings (killing hundreds of Hazara civilians), and attacks on Taliban officials. ISKP also attacks neighboring countries and plotted attacks in Europe (German Christmas market plot, Vienna plot). The Taliban fight ISKP militarily but lack the capacity to eradicate the group. ISKP has become a major international terrorism concern.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: ISKP membership: execution; facilitating ISKP attacks: execution; under international law: ISIS membership: prosecution in multiple jurisdictions
exceptions: Former ISKP members surrendering to Taliban under reconciliation offers treated differently from active fighters
Civilians in ISKP-affected areas are treated as potential victims rather than suspects in Taliban counter-operations

quiz.q: What was ISKP's most deadly attack in 2021 in Afghanistan?
options: A suicide bombing at the Afghan parliament
The Kabul airport bombing killing 183 people during the US evacuation
An attack on the US embassy in Kabul
Bombing of the Taliban Supreme Leader's compound
quiz.explanation: ISKP's most deadly 2021 attack was the suicide bombing at Kabul airport on August 26, 2021 — killing 183 people including 13 US service members and approximately 170 Afghan civilians who had gathered hoping to evacuate. The attack, occurring during the chaotic US withdrawal, demonstrated ISKP's capacity and intent to attack both Western forces and Taliban-affiliated areas.

laws.title: Healthcare System Collapse
laws.subtitle: Doctors Without Borders and WHO Emergency Response
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's healthcare system — partially built with international support between 2001-2021 — has largely collapsed. Over 80% of health facilities were funded by international donors; much of that funding was suspended after the Taliban takeover. Female doctors and nurses have been fired or fled. Hospitals lack basic supplies, medicines, and functioning equipment. Malnutrition is treated as triage in many facilities. MSF (Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders), WHO, UNICEF, and other organizations maintain emergency healthcare presence. Maternal mortality, infant mortality, and preventable disease deaths are all worsening.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: operating healthcare without Taliban authorization: closure; female healthcare workers in unauthorized settings: risk of arrest in some provinces
exceptions: Healthcare workers receive special authorization from Taliban to continue — female doctors in some provinces retained with restrictions
WHO and UNICEF emergency programs operate under negotiated access frameworks

quiz.q: What percentage of Afghanistan's health facilities were funded by international donors before 2021?
options: About 20%
Around 50%
Over 80% — most suspended after Taliban takeover
Only a few pilot facilities
quiz.explanation: Over 80% of Afghanistan's health facilities operated on international donor funding — a reflection of the internationally-funded state built between 2001-2021. When that funding was largely suspended after the Taliban takeover, the healthcare system faced collapse. WHO, UNICEF, and NGOs like MSF maintain emergency operations, but they cannot replace the full system that has broken down.

laws.title: National Parks and Natural Heritage
laws.subtitle: Band-e-Amir and Environmental Protection
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan established its first national park — Band-e-Amir — in 2009, protecting a remarkable series of deep blue natural lakes in the central Hazarajat highlands. Band-e-Amir was a tourist destination before the Taliban takeover. Under Taliban rule, tourism has virtually ceased. Wakhan Corridor — a remote strip connecting Afghanistan to China — has extraordinarily rich wildlife including snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep, and wolves. UNEP and WCS have worked on Afghan conservation. Environmental governance has entirely collapsed under Taliban rule — there is no functioning environmental ministry.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: poaching in protected areas: informal community-based penalties vary by region; land clearance: minimal enforcement capacity
exceptions: WCS and other conservation NGOs maintain limited presence in some areas under negotiated access
Local community rangers — informal system — continue in some protected areas

quiz.q: What was Afghanistan's first national park established in 2009?
options: Wakhan Corridor
Salang Pass Nature Reserve
Band-e-Amir — protecting remarkable series of deep blue natural lakes
Nuristan Forest Reserve
quiz.explanation: Band-e-Amir — established in 2009 — was Afghanistan's first national park, protecting a stunning series of naturally dammed deep blue lakes in the Bamyan Province. Before the Taliban takeover, the park was developing as a tourist destination with local community benefit. Under Taliban rule, the park's protection and tourism potential have been largely suspended.

laws.title: Taliban Security Forces and Violations
laws.subtitle: Badri 313 and Taliban Military
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's military forces — including the elite Badri 313 battalion — have been documented conducting extrajudicial killings, torture, and forced disappearances. The Haqqani Network (formally a Taliban faction, with its head Sirajuddin Haqqani serving as Interior Minister) has been designated as a terrorist organization by the US and is under individual sanctions. The Taliban have resisted international demands to account for former government officials and security forces. Military operations in Panjshir and Hazara areas have been accompanied by collective punishment. International criminal law provides potential accountability frameworks.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: Taliban soldiers killing civilians face internal discipline (inconsistently applied); no independent accountability mechanism; under international law: potential ICC prosecution
exceptions: ICC investigations subject to Taliban non-cooperation — practical enforcement very limited
US offers of reduced sanctions for individual Taliban members who provide information about terrorist organizations

quiz.q: What designation does the Haqqani Network hold internationally?
options: A recognized Afghan political party
A humanitarian organization
Designated as a terrorist organization by the US — with its head Sirajuddin Haqqani serving as Taliban Interior Minister
A regional development organization
quiz.explanation: The Haqqani Network is designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the United States — yet its head, Sirajuddin Haqqani, serves as the Taliban's Interior Minister. This creates an extraordinary situation where a minister of a de facto government is personally under US sanctions and designated as a terrorist. The Haqqani Network has conducted numerous deadly attacks in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

laws.title: Hazara Persecution
laws.subtitle: Ethnic and Religious Minority Violence
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's Hazara people — Shia Muslims who make up 8-10% of the population — face systematic persecution under Taliban rule. Hazaras have historically been discriminated against by Pashtun Taliban (Sunni). Under current Taliban rule, Hazara communities face targeted killings by ISKP (who view Shia as apostates), forced displacement from historical lands, banning of Hazara cultural and political organizations, and exclusion from Taliban governance positions. UNAMA has documented systematic targeting of Hazaras. The UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Afghanistan has described Taliban treatment of Hazaras as potentially constituting crimes against humanity.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: Hazara political organizing: arrest; Shia religious practices: restricted; ISIS-K attacks on Hazara mosques: Taliban claims to investigate but accountability minimal
exceptions: Hazara professionals in medicine and some technical fields may work with restrictions in some areas
Hazara communities in areas with local Taliban commanders of moderate interpretation have somewhat better conditions

quiz.q: What makes the Hazara people particularly targeted in Afghanistan?
options: They are the wealthiest ethnic group
Hazaras are Shia Muslims — targeted by both Sunni Taliban (persecution) and ISKP (genocidal attacks on mosques)
They are politically dominant
Hazaras are the largest ethnic group
quiz.explanation: Hazaras face a compound targeting: they are Shia Muslims in a country governed by Sunni Islamist Taliban (who have historically oppressed them) and are the target of genocidal attacks by ISKP (which views Shia as apostates deserving death). Multiple Hazara mosques and cultural events have been bombed by ISKP, killing hundreds, while Taliban governance excludes and persecutes Hazara communities.

laws.title: Hawala Money Transfer System
laws.subtitle: Informal Finance and Remittances
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's formal banking system has largely collapsed — most international banks severed correspondent banking after the Taliban takeover. The hawala system — an ancient trust-based informal money transfer network — has become the primary mechanism for remittances, humanitarian aid delivery, and trade finance. Hawala operators (hawaladars) transmit funds globally using a system of trust and offsetting transactions without physical money movement. USAID and UN agencies channel billions in humanitarian aid through hawala. The Taliban collect fees from and regulate hawaladars. Hawala provides financial lifeline but is also vulnerable to abuse for sanctions evasion.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: operating hawala without Taliban registration: fines; sanctions evasion through hawala: criminal prosecution in sanctioning countries; hawala fraud: severe IEA punishment
exceptions: UN OCHA and major humanitarian organizations authorized to use hawala under OFAC and EU sanctions humanitarian exceptions
Remittances from diaspora to families — primary hawala use — explicitly protected under humanitarian exceptions

quiz.q: Why has the hawala system become so critical in Afghanistan?
options: Taliban banned all banking
Formal banking has largely collapsed — hawala is the primary mechanism for remittances and humanitarian aid delivery
Afghans prefer hawala for cultural reasons
Hawala offers better exchange rates
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's formal banking system largely collapsed after the Taliban takeover — most international banks severed correspondent banking relationships due to sanctions risk. This forced reliance on hawala, the ancient trust-based informal money transfer system, for everything from family remittances to UN humanitarian aid delivery. Hawala now moves billions of dollars in and out of Afghanistan annually.

laws.title: Previous Afghan Constitutions
laws.subtitle: 2004 Constitution and Democratic Legacy
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's 2004 constitution — written with international assistance after the US-led intervention — established a democratic presidential republic with fundamental rights guarantees, an elected parliament (Wolesi Jirga and Meshrano Jirga), and an independent judiciary. Women had 27% reserved parliamentary seats. The constitution was in effect from 2004-2021 — overseeing four presidential elections (marred by fraud) and two parliamentary elections. The Taliban suspended the constitution in August 2021. Former President Ashraf Ghani fled Kabul as Taliban forces entered, becoming a symbol of the government's collapse.
laws.penalty: Under 2004 constitution (suspended): normal democratic governance penalties apply to violations; under Taliban: the 2004 constitution itself is considered illegitimate
exceptions: Afghan diaspora governments-in-exile reference the 2004 constitution as the legitimate framework
International recognition of the Taliban is conditioned on elements of the 2004 constitution's rights framework

quiz.q: What percentage of Afghan parliamentary seats were reserved for women under the 2004 constitution?
options: 27% — a significant female political participation requirement
Women were not allowed in parliament under the 2004 constitution
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's 2004 constitution reserved 27% of Wolesi Jirga (lower house) seats for women — a significant formal political participation requirement. This provision, created with international encouragement, gave Afghanistan a higher rate of formal female parliamentary representation than many Western democracies. All women's political participation has been eliminated under Taliban rule.

laws.title: NGO Restrictions and Aid Access
laws.subtitle: Taliban Bans on Female Aid Workers
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's December 2022 ban on female staff at NGOs (and subsequent ban on female UN staff in April 2023) severely disrupted humanitarian operations. Many NGOs suspended operations in protest. Some international organizations relocated female staff outside Afghanistan. The bans create operational problems: many Afghan women in need of assistance will not accept services from male aid workers — particularly health services. The UN and major NGOs have engaged in difficult negotiations with the Taliban, partially resuming some operations. The fundamental tension between principled humanitarian response and Taliban gender restrictions remains unresolved.
laws.penalty: NGO operating female staff in violation of Taliban ban: license suspension and staff arrest; international organizations bypassing ban: expulsion of organization from Afghanistan
exceptions: Healthcare settings — female medical staff have some authorization in some provinces under negotiations
National NGOs — distinction between international and national organization rules varies by province and commander

quiz.q: When did the Taliban ban female staff at NGOs and UN agencies?
options: Immediately when they took power in August 2021
December 2022 for NGOs; April 2023 for UN local staff
There is no such ban — female staff operate freely
Only Afghan female staff are banned — foreign female staff can work
quiz.explanation: The Taliban issued a ban on Afghan women working for NGOs in December 2022 and extended it to local UN staff in April 2023. These bans caused widespread suspension of humanitarian operations and are estimated to have significantly reduced the reach of aid to Afghan women and children who refused assistance from male aid workers due to cultural restrictions.

laws.title: Al-Qaeda and Terrorist Harboring
laws.subtitle: Doha Agreement Commitments and Violations
laws.fullDescription: The February 2020 Doha Agreement between the US and Taliban committed the Taliban to not allowing Afghan territory to be used by terrorist groups including al-Qaeda. The Taliban have demonstrably violated this commitment: al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri was killed by a US drone strike in central Kabul in July 2022, living in a house connected to Haqqani Network leaders — demonstrating al-Qaeda's continued presence in Taliban-controlled Kabul. The Taliban denied knowledge of al-Zawahiri's presence. Doha Agreement violation was the basis for ongoing US military pressure and sanctions.
laws.penalty: Under Doha Agreement: Taliban obligation to not harbor al-Qaeda — violation subject to US military response; under international law: state support for terrorism: UN Security Council sanctions
exceptions: Historical Taliban-al-Qaeda relationship predates the Doha Agreement — degree of current operational cooperation is disputed
Taliban claim to have separated from al-Qaeda while maintaining some historical personal relationships

quiz.q: How was al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri killed in 2022?
options: In a CIA raid in Pakistan
A US drone strike hit him in central Kabul — where he was living in a house connected to the Haqqani Network
He died of natural causes
Pakistani security forces captured and killed him
quiz.explanation: Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri was killed by a US drone strike in central Kabul, Afghanistan on July 31, 2022. He was living in a house connected to the Haqqani Network — a Taliban faction whose leader is the Taliban's Interior Minister. This directly demonstrated the Taliban's violation of the Doha Agreement commitment not to harbor terrorist groups, despite Taliban denials of knowing about al-Zawahiri's presence.

laws.title: Helmand River and Water Disputes
laws.subtitle: Afghanistan-Iran Hydro-Diplomacy
laws.fullDescription: The Helmand River — originating in the Hindu Kush and flowing through southern Afghanistan into Iran's Sistan Basin — has been a source of bilateral tension for decades. A 1973 treaty allocated water between Afghanistan and Iran. Afghan dam construction (Arghandab, Kajaki) and irrigation expansion have reduced flows into Iran. Iran has repeatedly protested insufficient water delivery, leading to border skirmishes in 2023. Climate change (drought) and poppy eradication (which reduced water-intensive cultivation) affect flows. The Sistan Lake in Iran has largely dried due to reduced Helmand flow. The Taliban has engaged with Iran on water but disputes continue.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: water theft from Helmand irrigation systems: community dispute resolution; dam sabotage: severe criminal penalties; Afghanistan-Iran water disputes: diplomatic
exceptions: Emergency humanitarian water releases during drought — informal practice recognized by both countries
Seasonal flow variations recognized as force majeure in 1973 treaty interpretation

quiz.q: What happened at the Afghanistan-Iran border in 2023 related to water?
options: A major dam joint project was announced
Border skirmishes over Helmand River water flows — Iran protested insufficient water delivery
An agreement resolved all water disputes
Afghanistan diverted the river entirely from Iran
quiz.explanation: Border skirmishes erupted at the Afghanistan-Iran border in 2023 over Helmand River water — Iran protested that Afghanistan was not delivering the water allocated under the 1973 Helmand River Treaty. The disputes reflect both deliberate water management choices and climate change reducing overall river flows. Iran's Sistan Basin has experienced severe drought and desiccation of Lake Hamoun partly due to reduced Helmand flows.

laws.title: Afghan Women's Resistance
laws.subtitle: Silent Protest and Underground Education
laws.fullDescription: Despite Taliban repression, Afghan women have maintained remarkable forms of resistance: underground schools operate secretly, teaching girls beyond 6th grade at personal risk; women have held silent street protests; female journalists document abuses through underground networks; and international advocacy by Afghan women in diaspora has kept global attention. Afghan female lawyers, civil society leaders, and politicians have spoken to UN bodies and parliaments. The Taliban have arrested and tortured female protesters. The international community has struggled to translate Afghan women's advocacy into effective pressure on the Taliban.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: organizing women's protests: arrest, torture, and long imprisonment; operating underground girls' schools: arrest of teachers and family; public female protest: beatings and detention
exceptions: Afghan women in diaspora countries can advocate freely under those countries' freedom of expression laws
Some female medical workers retained under Taliban authorization — creating a small authorized public presence

quiz.q: What forms of resistance have Afghan women maintained despite Taliban repression?
options: No resistance — all women have accepted Taliban rules
Underground schools, silent street protests, international advocacy through diaspora, documentation of abuses
Armed insurgency against Taliban
Economic strikes and boycotts
quiz.explanation: Afghan women have maintained multiple forms of resistance: underground schools secretly teaching girls beyond 6th grade, silent street protests (before these were banned and protesters arrested), international advocacy by diaspora female leaders to UN bodies and parliaments, and underground journalism networks. These courageous acts are conducted at serious personal risk — protesters have been arrested and tortured.

laws.title: Central Asian Energy Corridors
laws.subtitle: TAPI Pipeline and Regional Energy Links
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan is geographically positioned as a transit corridor for Central Asian energy — most notably the proposed TAPI pipeline (Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India) which would carry Turkmen gas through Afghanistan to South Asian markets. TAPI was under development before the Taliban takeover; status is now uncertain. Afghanistan also sits astride historic Silk Road trade routes connecting China with Central and South Asia. The Taliban have expressed interest in TAPI — which would provide transit fees — and in becoming a regional trade corridor. Insecurity and geopolitical complexity make these projects very challenging.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: pipeline interference or sabotage: severe criminal penalties; TAPI infrastructure protection is a Taliban stated priority
exceptions: Transit fee agreements under TAPI would be intergovernmental — Taliban authorization required
Emergency pipeline maintenance by international companies under negotiated security arrangements

quiz.q: What is the TAPI pipeline?
options: A Tajikistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India trade route
Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India gas pipeline — which would carry Turkmen gas through Afghanistan
Taliban-Afghanistan-Pakistan Infrastructure project
Trans-Asian Pipeline Initiative
quiz.explanation: TAPI (Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India) is a proposed natural gas pipeline that would transport Turkmen natural gas south through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India — providing Central Asian energy access and giving Afghanistan significant transit fee income. Under development before the Taliban takeover, TAPI's future is uncertain — though Taliban interest in the transit revenue has kept the project conceptually alive.

laws.title: Enforced Disappearances and Detentions
laws.subtitle: Taliban Detention System and Torture
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban operate a detention system outside any formal legal framework — arbitrary arrest, secret detention, torture, and enforced disappearances. Former government employees, civil society activists, journalists, and perceived opponents face detention without charge or trial. The Taliban's intelligence service (GIA — General Intelligence Authority) runs detention facilities where torture is documented by UNAMA and international human rights organizations. Family members are often not informed of detention or location. International pressure for specific releases has occasionally succeeded but systemic reform has not occurred.
laws.penalty: No accountability for Taliban detention abuses under IEA; international mechanisms: UN Special Rapporteur reports, ICC preliminary examination — practical enforcement extremely limited
exceptions: International pressure has secured release of some specific individuals — particularly those with diaspora family advocacy
Taliban commanders with personal relationships to detainees sometimes secure informal release

quiz.q: Which Taliban body runs secret detention facilities where torture is documented?
options: The Taliban Supreme Court
The Ministry of Justice
GIA — General Intelligence Authority
The Ministry of Interior (Haqqani Network)
quiz.explanation: The GIA (General Intelligence Authority) — the Taliban's intelligence service — operates secret detention facilities where UNAMA and international rights organizations have documented torture, enforced disappearances, and arbitrary detention of former government officials, journalists, civil society activists, and perceived opponents. The GIA operates outside any legal framework with no accountability mechanisms.

laws.title: Afghanistan's Future Governance
laws.subtitle: International Engagement and Long-Term Scenarios
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's future governance remains deeply uncertain. Scenarios include: continued Taliban rule with gradual international accommodation; collapse of Taliban governance from internal divisions or ISKP; emergence of new armed resistance (National Resistance Front in Panjshir); or negotiated political settlement. The international community faces the dilemma of engaging with Taliban for humanitarian access while refusing recognition that could validate their repression. Pakistan's relationship with Taliban (historical supporter, now increasingly strained by TTP attacks) is pivotal. China's economic interest (minerals, belt and road) makes it a potential key player. Afghanistan's future is deeply tied to regional geopolitics.
laws.penalty: No current enforcement mechanism for international governance norms in Afghanistan — any change will come through political or military processes
exceptions: Some Taliban commanders in areas with moderate interpretation are more open to international engagement
Local community structures (shuras, jirgas) provide informal governance that sometimes operates with more flexibility than central Taliban policy

quiz.q: What is the National Resistance Front mentioned in Afghanistan's governance outlook?
options: A Taliban sub-faction
An armed resistance movement based in Panjshir — one scenario for challenging Taliban rule
A UN-backed political transition body
A regional organization for Afghan governance
quiz.explanation: The National Resistance Front (NRF), led by Ahmad Massoud (son of the legendary commander Ahmad Shah Massoud), is an armed resistance movement based in the Panjshir Valley — historically resistant to Taliban control. The NRF represents one possible internal challenge to Taliban rule, though its military capacity is limited. Panjshir's mountainous terrain and historical resistance legacy make it a symbol of anti-Taliban struggle.

laws.title: Loya Jirga Tradition
laws.subtitle: Grand Assembly and Afghan Governance
laws.fullDescription: The Loya Jirga — a grand assembly of Afghan tribal leaders, elders, and representatives — is Afghanistan's traditional mechanism for resolving national crises, ratifying constitutions, and making major governance decisions. The 2003 Loya Jirga ratified the 2004 constitution. Emergency Loya Jirgas approved the Bonn Agreement (2001) and other key transitional decisions. Taliban have not used the Loya Jirga mechanism — preferring direct decree governance from the Supreme Leader. Some Afghans propose a traditional Loya Jirga as a mechanism for political resolution of the current crisis.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: unauthorized assembly of elders or Loya Jirga without Taliban approval: arrest risk; under previous system: violations of Loya Jirga process: constitutional court challenge
exceptions: Provincial jirgas (councils) continue to resolve local disputes with Taliban toleration in some areas
Tribal dispute resolution under customary Pashtunwali code recognized by Taliban in rural areas

quiz.q: What significant function did the 2003 Loya Jirga perform?
options: Elected the first Afghan president
Ratified Afghanistan's 2004 constitution
Approved the US military withdrawal
Expelled the Taliban from Kandahar
quiz.explanation: The 2003 Constitutional Loya Jirga ratified Afghanistan's 2004 constitution — the foundational document for the democratic system that governed Afghanistan until the Taliban's 2021 return. The Loya Jirga brought together thousands of delegates from across Afghanistan to debate and approve the constitution, representing an attempt to root the new governance framework in traditional Afghan consensus-building mechanisms.

laws.title: Famine and Food Insecurity
laws.subtitle: IPC Emergency Levels and WFP Response
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan faces catastrophic food insecurity — the World Food Programme (WFP) classifies large portions of the population at IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and some areas at IPC Phase 5 (Catastrophe/Famine). Drivers: economic collapse, drought, currency devaluation, destroyed supply chains, and the end of international aid that previously funded food purchases. WFP provides emergency food assistance to millions. The Taliban have created obstacles to aid delivery in some cases. Acute malnutrition rates among children are among the highest globally — with long-term consequences for child development.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: food aid diversion: harsh punishment; hoarding during famine: Taliban enforcement varies; humanitarian access obstruction: Taliban sometimes facilitate, sometimes obstruct
exceptions: WFP emergency operations have broad Taliban authorization — though specific delivery points may face obstacles
Community-based food sharing (an Afghan tradition) operates without formal regulation

quiz.q: How does the IPC classify Afghanistan's food security situation?
options: IPC Phase 1 — minimal food insecurity
IPC Phase 2 — some food stress
IPC Phase 4-5 — Emergency to Catastrophe/Famine
Afghanistan has no food security problems
quiz.explanation: Large portions of Afghanistan's population are classified at IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) food insecurity, with some areas reaching IPC Phase 5 (Catastrophe/Famine) — the highest levels of food crisis. This reflects the combination of economic collapse, drought, and destroyed aid systems following the Taliban takeover. WFP provides emergency food to millions, but needs exceed resources.

laws.title: Taliban Criminal Punishment — Flogging
laws.subtitle: Public Punishment and Sharia Implementation
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have conducted public flogging as judicial punishment for violations of their Sharia interpretation — including alcohol consumption, drug use, fornication, and various moral offenses. Floggings have been conducted in public spaces and recorded on video. International human rights organizations classify these as torture under international law. The Taliban Supreme Leader has decreed that judges must apply hudud (Quranic) punishments personally and not delegate them. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is one of very few countries in the world conducting systematic public corporal punishment.
laws.penalty: Alcohol consumption: flogging (40 lashes Taliban rule); fornication: flogging (100 lashes); drug use: flogging and imprisonment; 'immodest' dress: flogging
exceptions: Children cannot receive adult hudud punishments — modified sentences apply
Medical exemption for flogging theoretically exists but practical application is minimal

quiz.q: What did Taliban Supreme Leader Akhundzada decree about hudud punishments?
options: Judges should refer hudud cases to review committees
Judges must apply hudud punishments personally and not delegate them
Hudud punishments should be suspended during the international isolation period
Only the Supreme Court may authorize hudud punishments
quiz.explanation: Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada issued a decree ordering judges to personally apply hudud (Quranic) punishments — including flogging and amputation — rather than delegating to executioners. This directive aimed to ensure systematic application of corporal punishment across Afghanistan's Taliban-controlled court system, and has been implemented with public floggings documented across the country.

laws.title: Hindu Kush Mountains and Glaciers
laws.subtitle: Climate Change and Water Tower of Asia
laws.fullDescription: The Hindu Kush mountains — Afghanistan's dominant geographical feature — are sometimes called the 'water tower of Central and South Asia' because their glaciers and snowpack feed the major rivers of the region (Amu Darya, Helmand, Kabul River). Climate change is accelerating glacial retreat — threatening the seasonal water flows that millions depend on. The Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment (2019) found the region's glaciers could lose 2/3 of their volume by 2100. Natural disasters (avalanches, earthquakes) are severe in Afghan mountain areas. Afghanistan's geography makes it uniquely vulnerable to climate-induced water stress.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: formal environmental governance essentially non-existent in mountain regions; traditional community water management systems operate informally
exceptions: Emergency water infrastructure repair after natural disasters authorized without formal process
Traditional water jirgas manage irrigation distribution in mountain valleys

quiz.q: Why are Hindu Kush glaciers critical for the region?
options: They provide cooling air for all of Central Asia
They feed major rivers including Amu Darya, Helmand, and Kabul River — water sources for millions
They prevent earthquakes
They contain valuable minerals
quiz.explanation: The Hindu Kush glaciers and snowpack serve as the 'water tower' for Central and South Asia — seasonally releasing meltwater that feeds major rivers including the Amu Darya, Helmand, and Kabul River. These rivers are the primary water sources for agriculture in Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Pakistan, and Iran. Climate-driven glacial retreat threatens the long-term water security of the entire region.

laws.title: Legacy of Soviet Invasion and Cold War
laws.subtitle: 1979-1989 Soviet War and Its Consequences
laws.fullDescription: The Soviet Union's 1979 invasion of Afghanistan and the subsequent 10-year war fundamentally shaped modern Afghan history. The CIA-funded mujahideen resistance (including early support for figures who later founded al-Qaeda) drove the Soviets out but left Afghanistan with millions of weapons, millions of land mines, destroyed infrastructure, and millions of refugees. The Cold War proxy conflict killed 1-2 million Afghans and displaced over 5 million. Following Soviet withdrawal, Afghanistan fell into civil war (1989-1996), leading to the Taliban's first rise to power. The Soviet war's legacy — weapons, divisions, and extremism — continues to shape Afghanistan today.
laws.penalty: Historical Soviet-era violations: no accountability; land mines from Soviet era: ongoing casualty cause — demining programs reduce risk
exceptions: Soviet-era land mine removal operations by HALO Trust and Mines Advisory Group continue under special access
Historical Soviet-era weapons now illegal to possess privately — Taliban enforcing disarmament except their own forces

quiz.q: What long-term legacy of the Soviet-Afghan War continues to cause casualties?
options: Soviet tanks left abandoned
Millions of land mines from Soviet-era — killing and injuring civilians decades later
Soviet-built dams collapsing
Radioactive contamination from Soviet weapons
quiz.explanation: Millions of land mines laid during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979-1989) continue to cause casualties decades later — making Afghanistan one of the world's most mine-contaminated countries. HALO Trust, Mines Advisory Group, and UN Mine Action Service have cleared tens of millions of mines, but significant contamination remains in rural areas. Mines kill or maim dozens of Afghans monthly, particularly children.

laws.title: Saffron and Agricultural Exports
laws.subtitle: High-Value Crops as Poppy Alternatives
laws.fullDescription: In the post-opium environment, Afghan saffron — the world's most expensive spice — has emerged as a potential high-value alternative crop. Afghanistan's Herat and Farah provinces produce premium saffron. Before the Taliban ban disruption, pomegranates, grapes, almonds, pine nuts (chirk), and dried fruits were significant agricultural exports. Afghanistan had strong pomegranate exports to India, Pakistan, and regional markets. Taliban rule has complicated agricultural trade — certification, border management, and banking limitations affect export capacity. The potential for legal high-value agriculture has not been fully developed.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: agricultural export violations: Taliban customs enforcement; misrepresentation of product quality: informal market sanctions; illegal cross-border agricultural trade: customs penalties
exceptions: Subsistence farming and local market sales exempt from export certification requirements
Emergency seed distribution programs during food crisis operate under humanitarian exemptions

quiz.q: What high-value agricultural product is Afghanistan known for producing in Herat and Farah provinces?
options: Vanilla
Cardamom
Saffron — the world's most expensive spice
Turmeric
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's Herat and Farah provinces produce premium quality saffron — the world's most expensive spice by weight, made from the dried stigmas of crocus flowers. Afghan saffron has been gaining recognition in global markets as a high-value alternative to opium poppy, providing rural farmers with legitimate income. However, banking limitations, trade access, and the general economic crisis under Taliban rule constrain its development.

laws.title: Minority Religious Persecution
laws.subtitle: Sikhs, Hindus, and Christians in Afghanistan
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's tiny non-Muslim minorities — Sikhs (a few dozen remaining from thousands historically), Hindus, and Christians (mostly underground converts) — face severe persecution under Taliban rule. The Sikh community had maintained a presence in Afghanistan for centuries; most fled after repeated attacks and harassment. The lone Afghan Sikh who previously held a parliamentary seat under the democratic system has fled. The last Sikh gurdwara (temple) in Kabul was attacked in 2020 (pre-Taliban by ISIS-K) killing 25 worshippers. Under Taliban, Christians face execution if discovered as converts.
laws.penalty: Apostasy (Muslim converting to Christianity): death penalty under Taliban's Sharia interpretation; non-Muslim practicing religion openly: harassment, property confiscation, potential imprisonment; preaching to Muslims: death penalty
exceptions: Foreign diplomats of non-Muslim faith may practice religion privately on diplomatic premises
Historically recognized Sikh and Hindu communities had some tolerated presence — now essentially destroyed

quiz.q: What happened to Afghanistan's Sikh community?
options: They have prospered under Taliban rule
The historic Sikh community numbering thousands has dwindled to a few dozen — most fled after attacks and harassment
Sikhs remain a significant community in Kandahar
The Taliban guarantee Sikh rights under their constitution
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's Sikh community — once numbering in the thousands, maintaining gurdwaras and livelihoods for generations — has dwindled to only a few dozen people. Most fled following decades of persecution, the 2020 ISIS-K attack on Kabul's last major gurdwara (killing 25), and the Taliban's 2021 return. The practical erasure of this ancient community represents a devastating cultural and religious loss.

laws.title: Mental Health Crisis
laws.subtitle: Trauma, Poverty, and Taliban Restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan faces a severe and largely unaddressed mental health crisis. Decades of war, displacement, violence, and trauma have created enormous psychiatric need. Under Taliban rule, the already minimal mental health infrastructure has largely collapsed. Female mental health workers (who provided most mental health services to women) have been dismissed. Suicide rates, particularly among women and girls facing the loss of rights, education, and opportunities, have reportedly increased. WHO and NGOs provide very limited mental health services. Social support systems — family, community — remain the primary (and inadequate) response.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: suicide is a religious sin — family faces social stigma; mental health services are stigmatized; no formal mental health law
exceptions: Religious counseling for mental distress is the Taliban-accepted approach — imams and religious scholars serve informal mental health roles
International NGO mental health programs operate in limited areas under negotiated access

quiz.q: What impact has Taliban rule had on mental health services for women?
options: Mental health services have expanded under Taliban
Female mental health workers have been dismissed — depriving women of most mental health services
Mental health is not a problem in Afghanistan
Only foreign female mental health workers are restricted
quiz.explanation: Female mental health workers — who provided most mental health services to women (who largely cannot be served by male practitioners under cultural norms) — have been dismissed under Taliban employment bans. This has deprived Afghan women of virtually all professional mental health support at a time when stress, trauma, and despair are intensifying due to the loss of rights, education, and future prospects.

laws.title: Energy Infrastructure
laws.subtitle: Power Imports and DABS Electricity
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's electricity system — DABS (Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat) — imports power from neighboring Central Asian countries (Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Iran, Turkmenistan) and has some domestic hydro and diesel generation. Power supply is extremely limited — most Afghans have electricity for only a few hours daily, if at all. The Taliban have prioritized electricity supply, paying for imports with mineral exports and customs revenue. Power outages affect all economic activity. Rural electrification is minimal. Solar power has expanded informally — solar panels are widely used for small-scale power where grid electricity is unavailable.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: DABS payment arrears: service cuts (Taliban prioritize maintaining service to urban areas); electricity theft: informal punishment; unauthorized power generation above household scale: requires Taliban authorization
exceptions: Solar home systems for household use are widely tolerated without formal licensing
Emergency power for hospitals and essential services receives priority allocation without payment requirement

quiz.q: From which countries does Afghanistan primarily import electricity?
options: China and Russia
Saudi Arabia and UAE
Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Iran, and Turkmenistan — Central Asian neighbors
Pakistan and India
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan imports most of its electricity from neighboring Central Asian countries — Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Iran. This dependence on electricity imports makes Afghanistan vulnerable to payment disputes, geopolitical tensions, and supply disruptions. The Taliban have generally maintained electricity import payments using customs revenue and mineral exports, recognizing power supply as essential for urban stability.

laws.title: Post-2001 State Building Assessment
laws.subtitle: Lessons from 20 Years of International Intervention
laws.fullDescription: The 20-year US and NATO-led state building project in Afghanistan (2001-2021) is now widely assessed as a failure — despite the largest reconstruction investment in history. Assessments identify key failures: building an Afghan state modeled on Western institutions without local legitimacy, massive corruption enabled by international funding flows, failure to address Pakistani support for Taliban, underestimating Taliban resilience, and the fundamental contradiction between fighting a counterinsurgency while nation-building. Some positive legacies remain: the generation educated between 2001-2021, women who achieved professional skills, and democratic norms internalized by some Afghans.
laws.penalty: Historical accountability for state-building failures: pursued through SIGAR (US Inspector General) audits; no formal criminal accountability for program failures
exceptions: Afghan professionals educated during 2001-2021 carry institutional knowledge in exile — a human capital diaspora
Democratic norms among younger Afghans persist despite Taliban repression
laws.sourceLabel: SIGAR — US Inspector General for Afghanistan

quiz.q: What does SIGAR document about the Afghan reconstruction effort?
options: SIGAR found the reconstruction was a complete success
SIGAR audits documented widespread waste, fraud, and abuse in the USD 145+ billion reconstruction spending
SIGAR praised US military strategy exclusively
SIGAR was never allowed to investigate Afghanistan
quiz.explanation: SIGAR (Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction) issued hundreds of reports documenting widespread waste, fraud, and abuse in the USD 145+ billion US reconstruction investment. SIGAR reports found programs that built schools without students, military bases without soldiers, and infrastructure projects that collapsed or were abandoned. SIGAR's work provides the most comprehensive documentation of the reconstruction's failures.

laws.title: International Negotiation Strategy
laws.subtitle: UN Special Envoy and Engagement Debates
laws.fullDescription: The international community debates how to engage with the Taliban — with two broad camps: 'principled isolation' (no engagement without human rights progress) and 'pragmatic engagement' (maintaining channels to protect humanitarian access, prevent ISKP, and gradually moderate Taliban behavior). The UN Secretary-General appointed a Special Envoy for Afghanistan (Feridun Sinirlioğlu, 2024). The UN General Assembly resolution (2023) called for consultation with Afghans on a political process. Qatar and China maintain diplomatic channels. Some analysts argue the isolation has failed — emboldening Taliban hardliners; others argue engagement rewards repression.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: unauthorized foreign political engagement by Afghan civil society: arrest risk; international engagement without Taliban consent: Taliban may obstruct access
exceptions: UN Special Envoy operates under UNSC authorization with some protection for contacts
Humanitarian organizations engage Taliban at operational level without policy dialogue conditions

quiz.q: What debate shapes international engagement with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan?
options: Whether to recognize Afghanistan as a new country
'Principled isolation' (no engagement without rights progress) vs 'pragmatic engagement' (maintain channels for access and moderation)
Whether to send military forces back
Whether to support the National Resistance Front
quiz.explanation: The fundamental international debate about Afghanistan is between 'principled isolation' — refusing engagement until the Taliban meet human rights conditions including girls' education — and 'pragmatic engagement' — maintaining dialogue to protect humanitarian access, prevent ISKP, and potentially moderate Taliban behavior over time. Neither approach has definitively succeeded, and the debate shapes UN strategy, bilateral diplomacy, and humanitarian operations.

laws.title: Taliban Intelligence Services
laws.subtitle: General Intelligence Directorate (GIA) Abuses
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's General Intelligence Authority (GIA), housed in the former NDS building in Kabul, runs a surveillance and detention system targeting political opponents, civil society, journalists, and anyone perceived as threatening to Taliban rule. Phone communications are monitored. Former government employees must register. WhatsApp groups discussing politics have been infiltrated. Torture in GIA detention is documented by UNAMA — including beatings, electric shocks, and stress positions. GIA operations extend to targeting Afghan diaspora — attempting to intimidate critics abroad through threats to family members in Afghanistan.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: GIA detention is outside any legal framework — arbitrary, prolonged, with torture documented; no accountability mechanism exists
exceptions: Afghan diaspora activists outside Afghanistan operate under host country legal protection — though family in Afghanistan remain vulnerable
UN staff have some protection through diplomatic immunity provisions

quiz.q: How does Taliban intelligence target diaspora critics?
options: By tracking their social media posts globally
By attempting to intimidate critics abroad through threats to family members remaining in Afghanistan
By asking host countries to extradite them
By financial sanctions on diaspora Afghans
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's GIA attempts to silence diaspora critics by threatening and harassing their family members who remain in Afghanistan. When an Afghan diaspora journalist or activist speaks out against Taliban rule, their relatives in Afghanistan may receive visits, threats, or detention. This 'family hostage' approach is a documented intimidation tactic that chills diaspora Afghan advocacy.

laws.title: Narcotics Eradication Environmental Impact
laws.subtitle: Opium Ban and Agricultural Ecosystem
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's 2022 opium ban has had unexpected environmental dimensions. Poppy cultivation, while a drug crop, also supported rural agricultural ecosystems — providing income that maintained irrigation systems and rural farming capacity. Sudden removal of poppy income without alternatives caused agricultural abandonment and further food insecurity. On the positive side, poppy monoculture was intensifying water use in water-scarce regions — reduced cultivation may reduce water stress in some areas. The environmental impact of mass agricultural disruption (soil erosion, abandoned irrigation, land degradation) is ongoing.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: poppy cultivation: crop destruction; agricultural abandonment creating land degradation: not currently enforced
exceptions: Wheat and legal alternative crop cultivation actively encouraged by Taliban with some seed distribution
Emergency food crop cultivation given highest priority even on previously poppy-cultivated land

quiz.q: What unexpected agricultural consequence followed the Taliban's opium ban?
options: Massive increase in wheat production
Agricultural abandonment and further food insecurity — poppy income maintained irrigation systems
Environmental improvements everywhere
Formation of agricultural cooperatives
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's opium ban — while dramatically reducing a dangerous drug crop — had the unintended consequence of causing agricultural collapse in many areas. Poppy income had maintained irrigation systems, supported rural farming capacity, and provided cash for food purchases. Removing this income without alternatives caused farm abandonment, deteriorating irrigation, and further food insecurity in already impoverished rural areas.

laws.title: Child Rights and Child Soldiers
laws.subtitle: Recruitment and Protection Failures
laws.fullDescription: Children in Afghanistan face multiple rights violations: girls denied education; children facing forced marriage; child labor prevalent (estimated 30%+ of children working); and child soldier recruitment.
