The Taliban have a documented history of using boys in religious schools (madrassas) for military training and eventual recruitment. UN monitoring of children in armed conflict (CAAC) documents Taliban and ISKP recruitment of child soldiers. Orphanages under Taliban control have reportedly been used for religious-military indoctrination. UNICEF maintains some programs for child protection but access is severely limited.
laws.penalty: Under international law: child soldier recruitment: war crime under Rome Statute; under Taliban: no prohibition on military use of youth from madrassas; forced child marriage: no Afghan prohibition under Taliban
exceptions: UNICEF-supported programs for child protection operate in limited areas with Taliban authorization
Children who escape Taliban madrassa-military pipeline receive some protection through UN child protection mechanisms

quiz.q: What international law category applies to Taliban recruitment of children for military use?
options: Minor labor violation
Civil rights infringement
War crime under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court
Only domestic criminal offense
quiz.explanation: Recruitment and use of children in armed conflict is a war crime under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. The UN's Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) on Children and Armed Conflict documents cases of Taliban child soldier recruitment. The ICC's ongoing investigation into Afghanistan covers this and other potential war crimes.

laws.title: UN Mission in Afghanistan — UNAMA
laws.subtitle: Mandate, Limitations, and Human Rights
laws.fullDescription: UNAMA (UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan) was established in 2002 and remains the UN's primary Afghanistan presence. UNAMA's mandate includes political facilitation, human rights monitoring, and supporting humanitarian coordination. Under Taliban rule, UNAMA's operations are severely constrained: female staff are restricted, monitoring access is limited, and the Taliban have at times demanded UNAMA's departure. The UN Security Council has repeatedly renewed UNAMA's mandate over Taliban objections. UNAMA's human rights documentation — published in regular reports — provides the most systematic record of Taliban abuses despite access limitations.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of UNAMA operations: violation of UNSC mandate — subject to UN diplomatic pressure; UN staff safety violations: UNSC consideration
exceptions: UNAMA operates under negotiated arrangements with Taliban — not full freedom of movement
Humanitarian access facilitated by UNAMA often depends on local Taliban commander relationships rather than formal legal protection

quiz.q: What is UNAMA's primary constraint under Taliban rule?
options: UNAMA has left Afghanistan entirely
Severely constrained operations: female staff restrictions, limited monitoring access, Taliban threats of expulsion
UNAMA has full freedom of movement guaranteed by treaty
UNAMA only operates in non-Taliban areas
quiz.explanation: UNAMA's operations are severely constrained under Taliban rule: female staff face employment restrictions, field monitoring access to detention facilities and conflict areas is limited, and the Taliban have at times threatened expulsion of UNAMA entirely. Despite these limitations, UNAMA maintains presence and publishes the most systematic documentation of human rights conditions in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan.

laws.title: Drought and Crop Failure Cycles
laws.subtitle: La Niña, Monsoons, and Agricultural Vulnerability
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan experiences severe climate variability — alternating between devastating droughts and destructive floods. La Niña years bring drought to Afghanistan; El Niño years can bring excessive rainfall. The 2020-2022 drought was one of the worst in decades — destroying crops and forcing mass displacement. 2023 brought floods in some areas. Afghan farmers have extremely limited resilience — no irrigation, no crop insurance, no financial buffer. Climate change is increasing both the frequency of droughts and the intensity of floods. FAO emergency food assistance provides some support but cannot prevent food insecurity during bad harvest years.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: no formal weather-related disaster law — informal community solidarity norms operate; formal disaster declaration: Taliban may issue for aid access purposes
exceptions: Emergency humanitarian response during declared disaster events has Taliban authorization for accelerated aid delivery
FAO emergency seed distribution programs operate under humanitarian exemptions from normal agricultural controls

quiz.q: What climate pattern is associated with severe drought in Afghanistan?
options: El Niño years bring drought
La Niña years bring drought to Afghanistan — among the worst recently was 2020-2022
Neither pattern affects Afghanistan
Only Indian Ocean temperature drives Afghan drought
quiz.explanation: La Niña climate patterns are associated with drought conditions in Afghanistan — reducing the monsoon rains and mountain snowpack that Afghan agriculture depends on. The 2020-2022 drought coincided with La Niña conditions and was one of the worst in decades, contributing significantly to the humanitarian crisis already developing from the Taliban takeover and economic collapse.

laws.title: Property Confiscation
laws.subtitle: Taliban Asset Seizures and Land Grabs
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have conducted widespread property confiscation — seizing homes, businesses, and land from former government officials, civil society leaders, journalists, and perceived opponents who fled. Afghan property records were disrupted during the chaotic departure. Taliban commanders have allocated confiscated properties to their fighters and loyalists. Former government housing in Kabul was redistributed to Taliban members. Land grabs in rural areas — using Taliban authority to override traditional land rights — are documented. Women who fled with family members face complete loss of property rights. The property seizures are a significant human rights and rule of law concern.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: protesting property confiscation: arrest; claiming property rights against Taliban beneficiary: extreme danger; historical property claims: informal Taliban mediation sometimes available
exceptions: Taliban Supreme Court theoretically provides property dispute resolution — though practically inaccessible to victims of Taliban confiscation
Tribal dispute resolution in rural areas may address land disputes not involving Taliban members

quiz.q: What has happened to properties belonging to Afghans who fled after the Taliban takeover?
options: Properties are held in trust until owners return
Taliban have confiscated and redistributed homes, businesses, and land to Taliban members and loyalists
Properties are protected by UN oversight
Former owners can reclaim property through Taliban courts
quiz.explanation: The Taliban have conducted widespread property confiscation — seizing the homes, businesses, and land of Afghans who fled, including former government officials, journalists, and civil society leaders. These properties have been redistributed to Taliban fighters and loyalists. UNAMA has documented this as a systematic human rights violation that deprives returnees of their fundamental property rights.

laws.title: Groundwater Depletion
laws.subtitle: Kabul Aquifer and Urban Water Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Kabul's groundwater aquifer — the primary water source for the Afghan capital's 4-5 million residents — is critically depleted. Decades of population growth, urban expansion, and lack of regulated groundwater extraction have severely lowered water tables. Many hand pumps no longer reach water. Kabul faces a long-term water crisis that infrastructure investment cannot easily solve. Rural groundwater in agricultural areas is similarly depleted from irrigation. UNICEF and WHO provide emergency water in some areas. Climate change reduces recharge rates. The combination of population pressure and declining groundwater is an escalating crisis.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: unauthorized groundwater extraction (commercial scale): informal enforcement; water theft from shared wells: community dispute resolution
exceptions: Emergency water distribution by UNICEF and humanitarian organizations operates without groundwater extraction permits
Traditional community water management systems (karez — qanats) recognized without formal licensing

quiz.q: What is the primary water source for Kabul's millions of residents that is critically depleted?
options: The Kabul River — which still flows through the city
Imported bottled water
The underground aquifer — with depleting water tables forcing deeper wells
Kabul Reservoir — a large surface water storage
quiz.explanation: Kabul's underground aquifer provides the primary water source for the Afghan capital's 4-5 million residents. Decades of unregulated groundwater extraction combined with population growth have critically depleted the aquifer — lowering water tables to the point where many traditional hand pumps no longer reach water. This is an escalating urban water crisis with no easy solution.

laws.title: Digital Access and Mobile Phones
laws.subtitle: Internet, Mobile Networks, and Taliban Surveillance
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's mobile phone and internet infrastructure — built between 2001-2021 — provides connectivity for millions. Mobile phone ownership is widespread. The Taliban have not shut down mobile networks — they use them for governance communication and collect mobile operator taxes. However, internet is monitored and some content is blocked. WhatsApp and social media are widely used despite surveillance risk. Taliban fighters carry smartphones. The digital economy is minimal — limited by economic collapse and sanctions. Cryptocurrency use has been reported for transactions bypassing banking sanctions.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: anti-Taliban social media posts: arrest documented; encrypted communications: allowed but monitored; VPN use: gray area — not explicitly banned
exceptions: International organization staff using secure communications for operational purposes: informal toleration
Journalists with international media accreditation have some protection for communications tools

quiz.q: Have the Taliban shut down Afghanistan's mobile phone and internet infrastructure?
options: Yes — all communications are cut off
No — the Taliban use mobile networks for governance and collect taxes from operators while monitoring content
Taliban require special permits for all mobile phone use
Only foreigners are allowed to use phones and internet
quiz.explanation: The Taliban have not shut down Afghanistan's mobile phone and internet networks — instead using them for their own governance communication and collecting significant tax revenue from mobile operators. The Taliban monitor communications and arrest individuals for anti-Taliban social media posts, but the infrastructure itself continues operating as a key Taliban revenue source and governance tool.

laws.title: International Criminal Court Investigation
laws.subtitle: ICC Afghanistan Situation and War Crimes
laws.fullDescription: The International Criminal Court has an ongoing investigation into potential war crimes and crimes against humanity in Afghanistan — covering acts by Taliban, Afghan security forces, AND US/NATO forces (including alleged CIA torture at black sites and US military attacks on protected sites). The ICC investigation was reopened in full in 2022 after initially being challenged by the US. In practice, ICC investigations into Taliban conduct are severely constrained by non-cooperation. The investigation theoretically covers the most serious violations — execution of former government officials, torture, gender persecution as potential crimes against humanity, and ISKP attacks targeting civilians.
laws.penalty: ICC jurisdiction: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide — sentences up to life imprisonment; Taliban non-cooperation: limited practical enforcement; arrest warrants would make Taliban officials subject to arrest in ICC member states
exceptions: Complementarity principle applies — ICC only acts if Afghanistan (IEA) fails to genuinely prosecute; given IEA governance, this threshold is easily met
ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authorization needed before arrest warrants issued — process takes years

quiz.q: Which forces are covered by the ICC's Afghanistan investigation — not just the Taliban?
options: Only Taliban forces
Only Taliban and Afghan government forces
Taliban, Afghan security forces, AND US/NATO forces — including alleged CIA torture at black sites
Only ISKP (ISIS-K)
quiz.explanation: The ICC's Afghanistan investigation covers potential war crimes and crimes against humanity by all parties to the conflict — Taliban, Afghan National Security Forces, AND US and NATO forces (including alleged CIA torture at black sites and attacks on medical facilities). The US withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2020 partly in response to this investigation, though the ICC asserts jurisdiction regardless.

laws.title: Taliban Youth Radicalization
laws.subtitle: Madrassa System and Military Recruitment
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's educational system centers on religious madrassas — which now serve as the primary schooling for millions of Afghan boys. Madrassa curriculum focuses on Quranic memorization, religious studies, and Taliban ideology. Independent and secular education is suppressed. The madrassa-to-military pipeline creates a generation of young men trained primarily for religious-ideological warfare. International concerns focus on Afghan madrassas producing the next generation of Taliban fighters and potentially global jihadist recruits. Female education being banned ensures girls receive no formal education whatsoever — creating a generation of unschooled young women.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: attending non-Taliban-approved schools: closure; madrassa dropout: social pressure and Taliban monitoring; girls attending any school above 6th grade: teachers arrested
exceptions: Some urban areas allow limited secular technical education for boys — particularly for subjects considered useful for economic function
Religious education for girls (Quranic studies, basic Islamic knowledge) continues in some madrassa settings

quiz.q: What is the primary concern about the Taliban's madrassa-centric education system?
options: Madrassas are too expensive for poor families
Creating a generation trained primarily for religious-ideological warfare rather than economic and social development
Madrassas don't teach enough Arabic
Boys receive too much education compared to girls
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's madrassa-centric education system creates a generation of Afghan boys trained primarily in religious ideology and military preparation rather than the economic and social skills needed for development. Combined with the complete ban on girls' formal education, Afghanistan is creating a generation with severely limited human capital — creating decades-long economic and social consequences.

laws.title: Previous Democratic Leaders in Exile
laws.subtitle: Afghan Government-in-Exile Concepts
laws.fullDescription: Former Afghan leaders and officials live in exile — with varying levels of organized political activity. Former President Ashraf Ghani (who fled as Taliban entered Kabul) lives in UAE. Former Vice President Amrullah Saleh declared himself Acting President from exile. Former Chief Executive Abdullah Abdullah engages in international advocacy. Ahmad Massoud (National Resistance Front) operates from Tajikistan. These exiled figures lack unified leadership and international recognition but maintain networks within Afghanistan. No government-in-exile has been formally established or recognized. Their political future depends on whether Taliban governance eventually fails.
laws.penalty: Exiled Afghan officials participating in peaceful political advocacy are protected under host country laws; Taliban consider them enemies — family members in Afghanistan face risk
exceptions: Exiled officials have no formal legal status vis-à-vis the IEA
Host countries provide protection to Afghan exiles under asylum and humanitarian protection frameworks

quiz.q: What did former Afghan Vice President Amrullah Saleh declare from exile?
options: His retirement from politics
That he recognized the Taliban government
That he was Acting President of Afghanistan from exile
His plan to return to Afghanistan and negotiate
quiz.explanation: Former Vice President Amrullah Saleh declared himself Acting President of Afghanistan from exile — arguing that under the Afghan constitution, if the president was unable to serve (Ghani having fled), the vice president becomes acting president. Though no country recognized this claim, it represented a continued assertion of the democratic government's constitutional legitimacy against the Taliban's takeover.

laws.title: Afghan Currency and Inflation
laws.subtitle: Afghani Exchange Rate and Economic Stabilization
laws.fullDescription: Surprisingly, the Afghan afghani (AFN) has relatively stabilized under Taliban rule — the central bank (Da Afghanistan Bank) has managed to maintain the currency, partly by allowing the sale of USD brought in by the US government for humanitarian purposes. WFP and UN agencies inject hundreds of millions in USD annually through the humanitarian response — which feeds into the currency market. However, purchasing power for ordinary Afghans has collapsed — prices for basic goods increased dramatically while incomes fell or disappeared. The currency situation is better than feared, but underlying economic conditions remain catastrophic.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: currency manipulation: Da Afghanistan Bank enforcement; unauthorized foreign exchange dealing: criminal prosecution; counterfeiting: severe Taliban punishment
exceptions: Humanitarian USD injections by UN and NGOs are necessary for economy function — Taliban accommodate despite ideological tensions
Hawala operators perform essential currency exchange functions under Taliban registration but without formal banking regulation

quiz.q: Why has the Afghan afghani currency stabilized better than expected under Taliban rule?
options: Taliban economic policies are well-designed
WFP and UN humanitarian USD injections into the economy help maintain currency stability
Saudi Arabia is propping up the currency
Taliban printed large amounts of new money
quiz.explanation: The Afghan afghani has stabilized somewhat better than expected largely because WFP, UN agencies, and international NGOs inject hundreds of millions of US dollars annually through humanitarian operations — which flow into the currency market and provide demand for the afghani. This USD infusion creates a paradox: international aid that cannot flow through the Taliban government indirectly stabilizes Taliban-governed economy.

laws.title: Pakistan-Taliban Tensions
laws.subtitle: TTP and Durand Line Dispute
laws.fullDescription: Pakistan — once the Taliban's primary patron — has seen relations deteriorate sharply since 2021. The Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP/Pakistani Taliban) has dramatically increased attacks inside Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban takeover, using Afghan territory as a base. Pakistan blames Afghan Taliban for not suppressing TTP. Durand Line (Pakistan-Afghanistan border, disputed by all Afghan governments) tensions persist — Afghan Taliban have attacked Pakistani frontier posts. Pakistan conducted airstrikes inside Afghanistan in 2024 targeting TTP. The Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship is now characterized by mutual suspicion and cross-border violence rather than cooperation.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: Pakistani Taliban (TTP) operations — Taliban formally oppose TTP but enforcement is limited; border violations: military response possible
exceptions: Informal trade across Durand Line continues despite official tensions
Humanitarian goods cross the border under both governments' tolerance

quiz.q: What has deteriorated in Pakistan-Taliban relations since 2021?
options: Pakistan increased support for Taliban
Pakistan-Taliban relations have deteriorated due to TTP attacks inside Pakistan using Afghan territory as base, and Durand Line tensions
Pakistan has recognized the Taliban government but relations are tense
Taliban cut off all trade with Pakistan
quiz.explanation: Pakistan-Taliban relations have deteriorated significantly since 2021. The Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) dramatically increased attacks inside Pakistan from Afghan bases, while Afghan Taliban declined to suppress their Pakistani brethren. Border skirmishes along the disputed Durand Line added to tensions. Pakistan conducted airstrikes inside Afghanistan in 2024 — a remarkable shift from the relationship of patron-client that previously characterized Pakistan-Taliban ties.

laws.title: Afghan Civil Society Underground
laws.subtitle: Secret Networks and Resistance
laws.fullDescription: Despite Taliban repression, Afghan civil society continues — underground. Women's networks operate secretly, maintaining educational programs, psychological support, and advocacy networks. Journalists document abuses through encrypted communications to international media. Human rights monitors feed information to UNAMA and NGOs. Underground libraries and art projects keep cultural life alive. Young Afghans use social media (with VPNs) to connect with the world. The Taliban conduct raids on underground education programs, arresting teachers. But the human spirit of resistance — educated Afghans refusing to simply accept Taliban rule — represents a civil society that continues despite enormous risk.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: operating underground civil society: arrest, torture, imprisonment; providing information to international human rights groups: arrest; maintaining underground education: severe punishment
exceptions: Afghan diaspora civil society in other countries operates freely under host country laws
Some Taliban commanders with more moderate views tolerate limited civil society in their areas — inconsistent and unpredictable

quiz.q: How does Afghan civil society continue to operate under Taliban rule?
options: It has been completely suppressed — no civil society remains
Secretly — through underground education networks, encrypted journalism, and covert human rights monitoring at great personal risk
Openly — Taliban allow civil society if it avoids politics
Only international NGOs maintain civil society functions
quiz.explanation: Afghan civil society continues underground at great personal risk: secret women's education networks, encrypted journalism feeding information to international media, covert human rights monitoring for UNAMA, underground cultural preservation, and youth using VPNs to maintain global connections. Taliban raids on these networks lead to arrest and torture, but the civil society spirit persists among Afghans who refuse to simply accept Taliban rule.

laws.title: Landmine Contamination
laws.subtitle: HALO Trust and Mine Action
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan is one of the world's most heavily landmine-contaminated countries — with tens of millions of mines laid during Soviet occupation, civil war, and post-2001 conflict. HALO Trust, Mines Advisory Group (MAG), and the UN Mine Action Service (UNMAS) conduct demining operations. Since 2001, over 17 million mines have been cleared — but significant contamination remains. New mines were laid by Taliban during the 2001-2021 conflict; ISKP continues to use IEDs (improvised explosive devices). Land mines kill and injure dozens of Afghans monthly — disproportionately children. Under Taliban, international demining continues — one of few programs with consistent access.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: mine laying in civilian areas: theoretically prohibited under Geneva Conventions — practical enforcement absent; mine clearance organizations operate with Taliban authorization
exceptions: International demining organizations (HALO, MAG, UNMAS) have consistent Taliban access — one of the best-maintained humanitarian programs
Emergency mine clearance after IED incidents authorized without standard operational permits

quiz.q: How many mines have been cleared in Afghanistan since 2001?
options: About 1 million
Around 5 million
Over 17 million mines — yet significant contamination remains
All mines have been cleared
quiz.explanation: Over 17 million mines have been cleared in Afghanistan since 2001 by HALO Trust, Mines Advisory Group, UN Mine Action Service, and other demining organizations — a remarkable achievement. However, significant contamination remains, with new mines and IEDs continuously added during the 2001-2021 conflict and IED campaigns. Afghanistan is one of the few humanitarian programs where demining continues consistently under Taliban authorization.

laws.title: Drug Addiction Crisis
laws.subtitle: Afghan Drug Users and Treatment
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has one of the world's highest rates of drug use — an estimated 3 million Afghans use drugs (heroin, opium, hashish, methamphetamine). This addiction crisis predates Taliban rule but has worsened with economic collapse and despair. Children as young as 10 are reported using drugs. Under Taliban rule, drug treatment centers have been closed or restricted. The Taliban use forced detoxification (without medical support) as their primary 'treatment' approach — which is medically dangerous. UN and NGO harm reduction and treatment programs have extremely limited access.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: drug use: flogging and forced 'treatment'; drug selling: severe punishment including execution for major dealers; possession for personal use: flogging
exceptions: Medical opiate use (morphine for pain) at registered medical facilities permitted under health ministry authorization
International NGO drug treatment programs operate in very limited areas under humanitarian access

quiz.q: What is the estimated number of Afghans who use drugs?
options: About 100,000
Around 500,000
Approximately 3 million — including children as young as 10
Over 10 million
quiz.explanation: Approximately 3 million Afghans use drugs — one of the highest rates per capita globally. Heroin, opium, hashish, and increasingly methamphetamine are consumed. The addiction crisis has been driven by decades of conflict, easy availability of drugs during poppy cultivation era, poverty, and despair. Under Taliban rule, treatment access has been severely curtailed and their forced detoxification approach is medically dangerous.

laws.title: Freedom of Assembly
laws.subtitle: Taliban Restrictions on Public Gathering
laws.fullDescription: Freedom of assembly is effectively eliminated in Taliban-governed Afghanistan. Political meetings, protests, and public gatherings not authorized by Taliban are prohibited. Women's protests — there were several in 2021-2022 — were violently dispersed; organizers arrested and tortured. Unions, political parties, and civil society organizations cannot legally function. Religious gatherings (at mosques under Taliban-appointed imams) are permitted and encouraged. Traditional jirgas are allowed at the Taliban's discretion. International observers note Afghanistan has no functioning freedom of assembly.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized political gathering: arrest and torture documented; women's protest: beatings, arrest, and detention with torture; organizing banned assembly: long imprisonment
exceptions: Funeral gatherings: cultural practice generally tolerated unless associated with perceived opposition figures
Wedding celebrations: permitted subject to gender segregation requirements and Taliban-approved music restrictions

quiz.q: What happened when Afghan women held protests in 2021-2022?
options: Taliban allowed peaceful protests
Protests were protected under the Doha Agreement
Women's protests were violently dispersed — organizers arrested and tortured
Taliban negotiated with protest leaders
quiz.explanation: Women's protests in 2021-2022 — some of the only public demonstrations against Taliban rule — were violently dispersed by Taliban security forces. Women protesters were beaten, arrested, and subjected to torture in detention. Several protest organizers were held for extended periods. The Taliban's violent suppression of these protests effectively ended organized public demonstrations against their rule.

laws.title: Conservation Without Governance
laws.subtitle: Snow Leopards and Wildlife in Taliban Afghanistan
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's remote mountain ecosystems — Hindu Kush, Pamir, Wakhan — harbor globally significant wildlife including snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep, wolves, brown bears, and numerous endemic bird species. Before the Taliban, international conservation organizations (WCS, AWF) worked in Afghanistan. Under Taliban rule, most international conservation programs have suspended — leaving wildlife without formal protection. Snow leopards face increased poaching pressure. Marco Polo sheep hunting by wealthy international clients (which previously funded conservation) has ceased but so has conservation itself. The remote Wakhan Corridor remains relatively intact due to its inaccessibility.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: formal wildlife protection law essentially non-existent; poaching: informal community norms in some areas; wildlife trade: minimal enforcement
exceptions: Local community hunting norms in Wakhan Corridor provide informal protection for some wildlife
WCS maintains limited remote monitoring using camera traps in some areas

quiz.q: What iconic species inhabits Afghanistan's Hindu Kush and Wakhan Corridor?
options: Amur leopard
Bengal tiger
Snow leopard — facing increased poaching pressure with conservation program collapse
Cheetah
quiz.explanation: Snow leopards (Panthera uncia) inhabit Afghanistan's Hindu Kush and Pamir mountains, including the remote Wakhan Corridor. Afghanistan was one of the priority snow leopard range countries for international conservation before the Taliban takeover. With international conservation programs largely suspended, snow leopards face increased poaching pressure — their pelts and bones valued in traditional medicine and as luxury items.

laws.title: The Afghan Generation Lost
laws.subtitle: Impact on Children and Youth
laws.fullDescription: Demographers and development experts speak of Afghanistan's 'lost generation' — the cohort of children and youth who will grow to adulthood under Taliban rule without education, skills, or opportunities. An entire generation of girls will grow up without formal schooling above 6th grade. Boys receive only religious education in many areas. Even the boys' education is narrowly focused — preventing development of the human capital needed for economic modernization. Educated Afghans of the previous generation fled — taking their skills abroad. The cumulative human development loss will take generations to reverse, even if Taliban rule ends.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: no formal accountability for educational denial as policy; UN Special Rapporteur on Afghanistan describes girls' education ban as potential crime against humanity
exceptions: Underground education maintains some learning for some children
Afghan diaspora education programs serve some refugee children in Pakistan, Iran, and Europe

quiz.q: Why do experts call Afghan children growing up under Taliban rule a 'lost generation'?
options: They will be lost to emigration
They grow to adulthood without formal education, skills, or opportunities — particularly girls denied schooling — creating generations-long human capital loss
They are literally lost in conflict
They have forgotten their cultural heritage
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan's 'lost generation' refers to the children — particularly girls — who will grow to adulthood under Taliban rule without the education and skills needed for economic participation and human development. An entire cohort of Afghan girls will reach adulthood without having attended school beyond 6th grade. Even if Taliban rule eventually ends, reversing this human capital deficit will require generations of investment.

laws.title: Irrigation Systems and Karez Networks
laws.subtitle: Traditional Water Management in Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has an ancient water management heritage — the karez (qanat) system of underground horizontal wells has irrigated Afghan agriculture for millennia, drawing water from mountain aquifers. Thousands of karezes were damaged or destroyed during Soviet bombing and decades of conflict. Many rural communities depend on karez water. UNHCR, FAO, and humanitarian organizations have invested in karez rehabilitation. Under Taliban, limited karez maintenance continues — the agricultural necessity overrides governance considerations. Climate change and groundwater depletion are reducing the effectiveness of surviving karez systems.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: damaging karez infrastructure: community-based dispute resolution; stealing karez water: tribal conflict resolution; no formal water law enforcement
exceptions: Emergency karez repair after conflict or natural damage: humanitarian organizations authorized under OCHA coordination
Traditional jirga-based water sharing agreements recognized as legally binding by Taliban

quiz.q: What is a karez in Afghanistan?
options: A traditional Afghan tent dwelling
An ancient underground horizontal well system drawing water from mountain aquifers — irrigating Afghan agriculture for millennia
A traditional irrigation canal on the surface
A type of mountain spring
quiz.explanation: A karez (known as qanat in Persian and Arabic) is an ancient underground horizontal tunnel and well system that draws groundwater from mountain aquifers and delivers it to agricultural areas by gravity — no pumps needed. Afghanistan has thousands of karez systems, some thousands of years old, that have irrigated agriculture in otherwise dry areas for millennia. Conflict damage and groundwater depletion have reduced their effectiveness.

laws.title: Taliban International Relations
laws.subtitle: Diplomatic Engagement Despite Non-Recognition
laws.fullDescription: Despite no formal recognition, countries maintain practical engagement with Taliban Afghanistan: China and Russia have ambassadors in Kabul; Pakistan maintains close if strained relations; Qatar serves as an informal channel; India reopened its Kabul consulate; the US engages through Qatar. The UN maintains UNAMA with 300+ staff. Taliban officials travel to regional conferences. Countries need to engage for humanitarian aid, border management, terrorism prevention, and economic interests (China: minerals). The distinction between 'engagement' and 'recognition' creates complex diplomatic protocols where countries interact without legitimizing.
laws.penalty: For individual Taliban: travel to non-recognizing countries without UN sanctions waiver: arrest risk; for countries: informal engagement carries political cost but no legal penalty
exceptions: UNSC 'travel exemptions' allow certain Taliban officials to travel for peace negotiations
Qatar's hosting of Taliban political office creates a diplomatic channel recognized by most international parties

quiz.q: Which countries maintain ambassadors in Kabul despite not formally recognizing the Taliban government?
options: No countries maintain any presence
Only Pakistan
China and Russia maintain ambassadors in Kabul despite formal non-recognition
All neighboring countries have full diplomatic relations
quiz.explanation: China and Russia maintain ambassadors in Kabul despite not formally recognizing the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. This reflects both countries' pragmatic approach: China wants to protect its Afghan mineral interests and prevent ETIM (Uyghur separatist) safe havens; Russia wants to prevent Taliban-inspired extremism from affecting Central Asia. Both engage through presence without the political cost of formal recognition.

laws.title: Forced Marriage Under Taliban
laws.subtitle: Women's Rights and Marriage Law
laws.fullDescription: Under Taliban rule, protections against forced marriage that existed under the 2004 constitution have been eliminated. Taliban governance enables child marriage — girls as young as 12-14 are being married off, particularly in poor families who receive bride prices and reduce their number of dependents. Women who fled Afghanistan left behind sisters, mothers, and daughters facing forced marriage. Widows are particularly vulnerable — facing pressure to marry Taliban fighters under 'mutah' (temporary marriage) arrangements. Women cannot refuse marriage without risking family violence. The Taliban have proposed 'rules for marriage' that effectively eliminate women's consent requirements.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: women resisting forced marriage: beatings and imprisonment; family refusing Taliban fighter marriage demand: risk of property confiscation or violence
exceptions: Some urban families with moderate Taliban connections maintain informal ability to delay or refuse marriages
Women in Afghan diaspora countries have full legal protection against forced marriage under host country law

quiz.q: What is a 'mutah' marriage in the context of Taliban rule?
options: A traditional Pashtun wedding ceremony
A temporary marriage — widows face pressure to enter such arrangements with Taliban fighters
A marriage requiring bride price payment
A government-registered marriage
quiz.explanation: Mutah (temporary marriage) is an Islamic contract for a fixed-term marriage — controversial among Sunnis (practiced mainly in Shia Islam) but reportedly used by Taliban fighters who pressure widows and vulnerable women to enter these arrangements. Widows in Taliban Afghanistan face unique vulnerability — lacking male family protection, they are targets for forced mutah arrangements from which they have no legal recourse.

laws.title: Import and Export Under Taliban
laws.subtitle: Customs Revenue and Trade
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's primary domestic revenue comes from customs duties — collected at border crossings with Pakistan, Iran, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan. Afghanistan's imports: fuel (Iran), food, consumer goods (Pakistan, China). Exports: minerals (extracted artisanally), agricultural products (pine nuts, saffron, dried fruit), and — despite the ban — some residual opium stocks. The Taliban customs system replaced the previous government's revenue mechanism. Durand Line border (Pakistan) is a major customs collection point. Transit trade through Afghanistan provides additional fees.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: customs evasion: confiscation and imprisonment; smuggling: severe punishment; unauthorized cross-border trade: Taliban customs enforcement
exceptions: Humanitarian goods under UN and NGO authorization have customs exemption or reduced duties
Traditional cross-border tribal trade recognized under informal arrangements

quiz.q: What is the Taliban's primary source of domestic revenue?
options: Oil revenue from Amu Darya extraction
Taxes on agriculture
Customs duties from border crossings — the primary Taliban domestic revenue source
Income taxes on Afghan workers
quiz.explanation: Customs duties collected at Afghanistan's border crossings — particularly with Pakistan, Iran, and Central Asian countries — represent the Taliban's primary domestic revenue source. The Taliban have been relatively efficient at customs collection, replacing the previous government's mechanisms. This customs revenue funds Taliban military operations, basic governance, and increasingly teacher and civil servant salaries.

laws.title: Amnesty Violations
laws.subtitle: Broken Promise to Former Government Employees
laws.fullDescription: When the Taliban entered Kabul in August 2021, they announced a general amnesty for former government employees, security forces, and civil servants — promising no reprisals. Within weeks, UNAMA began documenting killings and disappearances of former officials, soldiers, and police. Former special forces members — who had fought Taliban for years — were particularly targeted. The Doha Agreement also contained commitments against reprisals. Both commitments have been systematically violated. The US provided lists of vulnerable Afghans during evacuation operations — and Taliban used some of this information to locate them.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: Taliban violations of own amnesty — no accountability mechanism; former officials in hiding: extraordinary vulnerability; those who accepted Taliban 'amnesty' in good faith: significant number killed
exceptions: Some former officials at lower levels have successfully integrated under Taliban rule
Taliban officials with personal relationships to former government figures have provided informal protection in isolated cases

quiz.q: What happened to the Taliban's announced general amnesty after taking Kabul?
options: The amnesty was honored — no reprisals documented
The amnesty protected everyone who surrendered within 30 days
The amnesty was systematically violated — UNAMA documented killings and disappearances of former officials within weeks
The amnesty was extended to include Taliban's opposition leaders
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's announced general amnesty for former government employees and security forces was systematically violated from the earliest weeks of their rule. UNAMA documented extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances of former officials, military personnel, and civil servants who stayed in Afghanistan trusting the amnesty. Former special forces members — who had combat experience fighting Taliban — were particularly targeted for elimination.

laws.title: Pakistan-Afghanistan Refugee Dynamics
laws.subtitle: 3 Million Afghans in Pakistan and Deportations
laws.fullDescription: Pakistan hosts approximately 3 million Afghan refugees — one of the world's largest refugee populations in a single country. Most are unregistered and live in urban areas. Pakistan's 2023 decision to deport undocumented Afghans created a humanitarian crisis — hundreds of thousands returned to Taliban Afghanistan in weeks. UNHCR appealed for protection; Pakistan insisted on enforcement. The returns created additional pressure on Afghanistan's already strained humanitarian system. Afghan refugees in Pakistan face regular harassment, arbitrary detention, and limited legal rights. The mass return has human rights implications given the conditions in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan.
laws.penalty: Pakistani law: undocumented Afghan presence: deportation; Afghan refugees in Pakistan: non-refoulement protections theoretically apply but Pakistan has not signed 1951 Refugee Convention
exceptions: UNHCR-registered refugees have some but not comprehensive protection from deportation
Afghans with Pakistani citizenship or legal permanent status have full rights as Pakistani nationals

quiz.q: What refugee protection principle did Pakistan's 2023 Afghan deportation campaign raise?
options: Right to family unity
Non-refoulement — the obligation not to return people to where they face persecution
Right to work permits
Right to education
quiz.explanation: Pakistan's 2023 campaign deporting hundreds of thousands of undocumented Afghans raised serious non-refoulement concerns — the international principle prohibiting return of people to countries where they face persecution or serious harm. UNHCR appealed for suspension, noting that returnees faced Taliban persecution. Pakistan, which has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention, argued that undocumented migrants must be returned regardless.

laws.title: Poppy Eradication Environmental Effects
laws.subtitle: Agricultural Land Use Change Post-Ban
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban's poppy eradication campaign — while dramatically reducing opium production — has had complex agricultural and environmental effects. Poppy requires irrigation, creating water-intensive but economically productive farming. With poppy removed, many farmers have abandoned fields or planted drought-resistant but lower-value subsistence crops. In some areas, abandoned poppy fields are being converted to wheat or vegetables under FAO alternative livelihood programs. The sudden agricultural transition without support creates soil erosion, irrigation system deterioration, and increased food insecurity. Environmental monitoring of post-poppy land use is severely limited.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: any return to poppy cultivation: Taliban eradication and imprisonment; land abandonment: no formal penalty but social consequences; agricultural law violations: Taliban enforcement
exceptions: FAO alternative livelihood programs provide seeds and support for legal crops — operating under humanitarian authorization
Emergency subsistence cultivation on formerly-poppy land authorized without standard agricultural permits

quiz.q: What agricultural challenge has the sudden poppy ban created?
options: Farmers converted directly to profitable alternative crops
Abandoned fields, deteriorating irrigation, and food insecurity — as poppy removal without alternatives left farmers with no viable income
Wheat production exploded — food security improved
Foreign companies invested in replacing poppy with other crops
quiz.explanation: The sudden poppy ban without adequate alternative livelihood support caused widespread agricultural disruption: farmers who depended on poppy income abandoned fields when they couldn't afford to plant alternative crops, irrigation systems began deteriorating without poppy cultivation income to maintain them, and food insecurity worsened in areas where poppy was the primary cash crop enabling food purchases. FAO alternative livelihood programs attempt to fill the gap but resources are insufficient.

laws.title: Traditional Dispute Resolution
laws.subtitle: Jirga, Shura, and Customary Law
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has a deep tradition of conflict resolution through jirgas (assemblies of elders, primarily Pashtun) and shuras (councils, broader usage). These traditional systems operate alongside — and often more effectively than — formal legal structures. Under Taliban rule, jirgas and shuras continue for family disputes, land conflicts, and community matters. The Taliban have a complex relationship with customary law — rejecting elements they consider un-Islamic while relying on jirga structures for community governance. Pashtunwali (the Pashtun customary code) shapes behavior even under Taliban governance in rural areas.
laws.penalty: Jirga decisions have social enforcement mechanisms — ostracism and social pressure; violation of jirga settlement: community violence possible; Taliban may invalidate jirga decisions inconsistent with their Sharia interpretation
exceptions: Jirga decisions on land and water disputes generally accepted by Taliban without review in rural areas
Traditional blood feud resolution through jirga (using blood money) recognized by Taliban as legitimate dispute resolution

quiz.q: What is Pashtunwali?
options: A Pashtun language dialect
A traditional Pashtun customary code governing behavior, honor, hospitality, and conflict resolution
A Pashtun musical tradition
A type of Afghan textile
quiz.explanation: Pashtunwali is the traditional customary code of the Pashtun people — a comprehensive set of norms governing behavior, honor (nang), hospitality (melmastia), revenge (badal), refuge (nanawatai), and conflict resolution. It operates alongside and sometimes in tension with Islamic law. Taliban, who are predominantly Pashtun, navigate a complex relationship with Pashtunwali — embracing some elements while rejecting those they consider inconsistent with their Sharia interpretation.

laws.title: Gender Apartheid — International Law
laws.subtitle: Crime Against Humanity Designation
laws.fullDescription: The UN Special Rapporteur on Afghanistan, Richard Bennett, has called for the Taliban's systematic persecution of women and girls to be recognized as 'gender apartheid' — a potential crime against humanity under international law. While the Rome Statute criminalizes 'gender persecution' as a crime against humanity, 'gender apartheid' is not currently a defined crime in international law. There are advocacy efforts to include gender apartheid in future international legal instruments. The ICC's Afghanistan investigation may pursue gender persecution charges. The Taliban's systematic, comprehensive, and sustained targeting of women as a class has no equivalent anywhere in the world.
laws.penalty: Gender apartheid as potential crime against humanity: ICC investigation ongoing; individual Taliban commanders may face future prosecution for gender persecution
exceptions: ICC complementarity principle: IEA will not prosecute its own leaders for gender persecution — opening ICC jurisdiction
No political solution or negotiation has successfully obtained Taliban commitments to reverse gender apartheid policies

quiz.q: What term has the UN Special Rapporteur used to describe Taliban treatment of women?
options: Gender discrimination
Gender inequality
Gender apartheid — a potential crime against humanity under international law
Gender imbalance
quiz.explanation: UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett has explicitly characterized Taliban treatment of women and girls as 'gender apartheid' — a systematic, comprehensive, and sustained elimination of women from public life with no equivalent anywhere in the world. Bennett has called for this to be recognized as a crime against humanity under international law, noting it goes beyond discrimination to constitute a fundamental attack on the human rights of half the Afghan population.

laws.title: China's Afghanistan Strategy
laws.subtitle: Minerals, Pipeline, and Belt and Road
laws.fullDescription: China is the most significant non-regional power engaged with Taliban Afghanistan. China's interests: preventing Uyghur ETIM separatists from using Afghan territory; accessing Afghanistan's enormous mineral wealth (copper, lithium, rare earths); and extending Belt and Road connectivity. China's CITIC group previously signed a copper deal at Mes Aynak (largest undeveloped copper deposit) — under review for development. Chinese companies are exploring lithium and other mining opportunities. China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) could potentially extend into Afghanistan. China has appointed an ambassador to Kabul while not formally recognizing the Taliban government.
laws.penalty: Under Chinese law: Chinese companies violating sanctions related to Afghanistan: criminal prosecution in China; Taliban reneging on Chinese investment agreements: arbitration and diplomatic dispute
exceptions: Chinese state-owned enterprises benefit from political risk coverage for investments in complex environments
Afghanistan's non-recognition status creates contract enforceability challenges — Chinese investors require special political risk insurance

quiz.q: What is China's primary strategic concern regarding Afghanistan?
options: Preventing refugee flows to China
Controlling the Wakhan Corridor border
Preventing Uyghur ETIM separatists from using Afghan territory as a base against China
Securing Afghanistan's oil reserves
quiz.explanation: China's primary strategic concern about Afghanistan is preventing ETIM (East Turkestan Islamic Movement) — Uyghur separatists wanted for attacks in Xinjiang — from using Afghan territory as a training and operational base. This concern drives China to maintain engagement with the Taliban, pressure them to suppress ETIM, and offer economic incentives (mining investment) in exchange for security cooperation.

laws.title: Women in Taliban Detention
laws.subtitle: Female Political Prisoners
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have detained women activists, protest organizers, journalists, and family members of critics. Women in Taliban detention face severe conditions: incommunicado detention, torture, sexual violence, and denial of legal representation. Several women's rights activists including Tamana Zaryabi Paryani and Parwana Ibrahimkhel were arrested after posting protest videos and held for months. Families are typically not informed of detention locations. International pressure has secured some releases — particularly of individuals with international connections. Women detainees face the additional vulnerability of having no independent legal recourse under Taliban governance.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: women activists detained: prolonged imprisonment without charge; families: risk of arrest for seeking information; legal representation: not permitted under Taliban practice
exceptions: International pressure and high-profile cases have secured some releases through diplomatic channels
Taliban have released some women after 'pledges' from male guardians to prevent future protests — a patriarchal intervention mechanism

quiz.q: How have some detained women activists secured release under Taliban rule?
options: Through Taliban courts that fairly adjudicated their cases
International pressure and diplomatic channels — particularly for high-profile cases with international connections
Through payment of fines
By converting to more conservative Islamic practice
quiz.explanation: Some high-profile women activists detained by Taliban have been released following intense international pressure and diplomatic intervention — particularly for individuals with significant international connections or profiles. Organizations like Amnesty International, HRW, and international diplomats have campaigned for specific individuals. Taliban have also released some after male guardians provided 'pledges' that they would prevent future protest activity — a paternalistic enforcement mechanism.

laws.title: Hazarajat and Minority Cultural Preservation
laws.subtitle: Hazara Cultural Heritage Under Threat
laws.fullDescription: The Hazarajat — the central Afghan highlands historically inhabited by Hazara Shia — represents a distinct cultural, linguistic (Hazaragi Persian dialect), and religious tradition. Hazara cultural institutions — museums, schools, cultural centers — have been closed or restricted under Taliban rule. Hazara-related historical sites have no protection. The Taliban destroyed the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 — a symbol of cultural erasure. Under current rule, Hazara cultural expression is suppressed. The UNESCO intangible cultural heritage of Afghan communities is threatened — traditional music, poetry, and arts face severe restrictions.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: Hazara cultural organizations: banned; traditional Hazara Nowruz (New Year) celebrations: restricted; teaching Hazaragi language outside Quran context: restricted
exceptions: Private family cultural preservation in home settings tolerated in some areas
Some Hazara cultural items recognized under UNESCO heritage frameworks receive international advocacy protection

quiz.q: What iconic act of cultural destruction did the Taliban commit in 2001 that became a global symbol?
options: Burning all books in the national library
Closing the Kabul Museum
Destroying the Bamiyan Buddhas — 6th century giant statues carved into cliffsides
Demolishing the Kabul sports stadium
quiz.explanation: The Taliban destroyed the Bamiyan Buddhas in March 2001 — two giant 6th century Buddhist statues carved into the sandstone cliffs of Bamiyan Valley, one standing 55 meters tall. The destruction, condemned worldwide, was carried out with explosives and artillery over several weeks. The Buddhas were UNESCO World Heritage sites representing Afghanistan's pre-Islamic cultural heritage. The act became an enduring symbol of Taliban cultural destructiveness.

laws.title: Urban Air Quality in Kabul
laws.subtitle: Wood Burning and Pollution Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Kabul has among the worst urban air quality in Asia — driven by massive wood and coal burning for heating (due to electricity shortages), vehicle emissions from a rapidly growing fleet of old cars, and dust. Winter air quality is hazardous — PM2.5 levels regularly exceed 300+ μg/m³ (WHO guideline: 15 μg/m³). The fuel wood demand is driving deforestation in surrounding mountains. Under Taliban, there is no meaningful air quality management. Poor air quality causes widespread respiratory disease — particularly affecting children and elderly. The economic collapse has increased reliance on wood burning as families cannot afford other fuels.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: no air quality enforcement; deforestation for fuel: informal community opposition; industrial emissions: minimal enforcement
exceptions: UNDP and NGO programs for fuel-efficient stoves reduce emissions while providing economic benefit — operating under humanitarian authorization
International aid for solar and renewable energy in Kabul reduces fossil fuel burning

quiz.q: What drives Kabul's severe winter air pollution crisis?
options: Industrial factory emissions
Dust storms from the desert
Massive wood and coal burning for heating due to electricity shortages, plus old vehicle emissions
Agricultural burning in surrounding fields
quiz.explanation: Kabul's severe winter air pollution is driven primarily by massive wood and coal burning for heating — a consequence of chronic electricity shortages that prevent electric heating. Millions of Kabul residents burn wood, coal, and even plastic and tires for warmth. Combined with emissions from an aging vehicle fleet and construction dust, Kabul's winter PM2.5 levels regularly reach catastrophic levels — among the worst in Asia.

laws.title: UNHCR and Refugee Determination
laws.subtitle: Refugees from Taliban-Ruled Afghanistan
laws.fullDescription: UNHCR has determined that Afghans fleeing Taliban rule have strong prima facie claims for refugee status under the 1951 Refugee Convention — particularly women, former government officials, journalists, civil society workers, and ethnic/religious minorities. Afghan asylum applications have surged in Europe, the US, Canada, and Australia. Countries debate asylum policies — Germany, UK, and others have grappled with deportation policies for Afghan failed asylum seekers (most courts have blocked deportations given security conditions). Afghan evacuation programs (by US, UK, Germany, Canada) created special immigration pathways. The Taliban has demanded refugee-hosting countries return Afghans.
laws.penalty: Afghan asylum seekers: subject to host country asylum law; Taliban demands returns: diplomatic pressure only — no legal mechanism to compel returns
exceptions: Afghans who collaborated with Western military forces have priority resettlement programs
SIV (Special Immigrant Visa) holders from US have separate fast-track legal status

quiz.q: What UNHCR determination affects Afghan asylum seekers globally?
options: UNHCR found Afghans can safely return
UNHCR has stopped processing Afghan claims
UNHCR determined Afghans fleeing Taliban have strong prima facie refugee claims — particularly women, former officials, journalists
UNHCR limited Afghan claims to those directly persecuted
quiz.explanation: UNHCR has issued guidance determining that Afghans fleeing Taliban rule — particularly women, former government officials, journalists, civil society workers, and ethnic/religious minorities — have strong prima facie (prima face) claims for refugee status under the 1951 Refugee Convention. This guidance has shaped asylum adjudications in dozens of countries, generally supporting protection for Afghan applicants who can demonstrate relevant risk factors.

laws.title: Child Marriage and Dowry Practices
laws.subtitle: Baad and Forced Marriage of Girls
laws.fullDescription: Under Taliban rule, child marriage — already prevalent — has dramatically increased. Economic desperation (driven by the humanitarian crisis) causes families to marry daughters for bride price payments. Girls as young as 8-9 are reportedly being married. 'Baad' — the practice of giving girls as compensation in dispute resolution — continues. The minimum marriage age for girls set in the previous legal system (16, eventually raised to 18) has been eliminated under Taliban governance. International child marriage statistics from Afghanistan are incomplete due to monitoring limitations, but all indicators suggest dramatic increases. UNICEF and humanitarian organizations document cases through underground networks.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: no prohibition on child marriage; under international law: child marriage is CEDAW violation; 'baad' practice: internationally condemned as trafficking
exceptions: Afghan women in diaspora countries protected from forced marriage by host country law
UNICEF protection programs for at-risk girls operate in limited areas under humanitarian access

quiz.q: What is 'baad' in Afghan traditional practices?
options: A type of traditional Afghan meal
Giving girls as compensation to resolve disputes between families — a form of child marriage
A wedding ceremony tradition
A form of blood money payment
quiz.explanation: Baad is the practice of giving girls (sometimes very young girls) as compensation to the opposing party in disputes between families — for example, after a murder or theft, the offending family may give a daughter to the victim's family to resolve the conflict. International law classifies this as a form of forced marriage and trafficking. Under Taliban governance, there is no legal prohibition on this practice.

laws.title: Flood Disaster Response
laws.subtitle: Monsoon Floods and Climate Disasters
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan experiences severe seasonal flooding — particularly from snowmelt in spring and monsoon rains in summer. Floods destroy villages, agricultural land, and infrastructure. Under Taliban rule, disaster response capacity is essentially non-existent — the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) is now a Taliban ministry with minimal resources. International humanitarian organizations (OCHA, WFP, UNICEF) provide emergency flood response. 2023 floods in Herat province killed hundreds and destroyed thousands of homes. Climate change is increasing flood intensity. Communities rebuilt after Soviet-era floods now face repeated disasters with no governmental support.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: no formal flood disaster law; informal community emergency systems operate; humanitarian organizations respond under OCHA coordination frameworks
exceptions: Emergency flood response operations authorized by Taliban under humanitarian coordination protocols
International disaster response organizations operate under blanket authorization during declared emergencies

quiz.q: What happened in Herat province in 2023 related to climate disasters?
options: A major earthquake destroyed the city
Severe floods killed hundreds and destroyed thousands of homes
A drought caused complete crop failure
An ISKP attack targeted flood response teams
quiz.explanation: Herat province experienced devastating floods in 2023 — killing hundreds of people and destroying thousands of homes in multiple flood events. The disasters exposed Afghanistan's near-complete absence of disaster response capacity under Taliban governance, with international organizations (OCHA, WFP, UNICEF) providing essentially all emergency response. Climate change is increasing flood intensity and frequency across Afghanistan.

laws.title: Taliban Media Control
laws.subtitle: State Media and Information Warfare
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban control the national broadcaster Radio Television Afghanistan (RTA) — now rebranded Radio TV Bakht — which broadcasts Taliban propaganda, religious programming, and official news. Women are banned from appearing on television. Music is banned from broadcast. International media (BBC Dari/Pashto, VOA, Radio Free Europe) provide alternative information through shortwave radio and online — critical information lifelines for Afghans. The Taliban jam some frequencies and block websites. Social media remains accessible with VPN. Foreign journalists operate under restricted credentials with Taliban media minders. Independent journalism operates underground.
laws.penalty: Broadcasting without Taliban authorization: criminal prosecution; reporting anti-Taliban content: arrest; listening to 'enemy' radio: socially dangerous but not yet systematically criminalized
exceptions: Foreign media accredited by Taliban ministry may operate within restrictions
BBC Dari and VOA maintain operating licenses despite content that contradicts Taliban narratives — Taliban accept some foreign media for diplomatic reasons

quiz.q: What are the Taliban's main restrictions on broadcast media?
options: Only news is restricted — entertainment can broadcast freely
Women banned from TV, music banned from broadcast, content must follow Taliban ideology — RTA broadcasts Taliban propaganda
All broadcast media is banned — only print media allowed
Only foreign language broadcasts are restricted
quiz.explanation: Taliban broadcast media restrictions include: women completely banned from appearing on television, music banned from radio and TV broadcasts, all content must conform to Taliban ideology and Islamic standards as interpreted by them, and the national broadcaster (RTA, renamed Radio TV Bakht) exclusively broadcasts Taliban propaganda, religious programming, and official news. Independent broadcasting inside Afghanistan is impossible.

laws.title: Taliban and Regional Stability
laws.subtitle: Spillover Effects on Central and South Asia
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's governance crisis under Taliban has significant regional spillover effects. Pakistan: TTP attacks have dramatically increased; drug trafficking route challenges. Iran: Afghan refugee burden; Helmand water dispute; drug trafficking through Iran. Central Asia: concerns about extremist spillover; Afghan refugees; drug trafficking. Russia: monitoring extremism; concerned about Central Asian instability. India: concerned about Pakistan-Taliban strategic relationship; reduced influence in Afghanistan. China: ETIM concerns; trade opportunities. The regional impacts of Afghanistan's crisis are reshaping security calculations across Eurasia — making Afghanistan a central, not peripheral, security concern.
laws.penalty: Spillover effects handled through bilateral diplomacy and security cooperation; no formal legal framework for managing Afghanistan's destabilizing regional impacts
exceptions: Regional security cooperation (SCO, CSTO) provides some coordination framework for addressing Afghanistan spillover
Humanitarian corridors for aid and refugees operate under multilateral coordination

quiz.q: What regional security concern has Afghanistan's Taliban governance created for Pakistan specifically?
options: Afghan refugees overwhelming Pakistani cities
Dramatically increased TTP (Pakistani Taliban) attacks inside Pakistan using Afghan territory as a base
Afghanistan cutting off trade with Pakistan
Taliban demanding Pakistan join the Islamic Emirate
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's return to power dramatically emboldened and strengthened the TTP (Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan — Pakistani Taliban), who dramatically increased attacks inside Pakistan from Afghan bases. The TTP killed hundreds of Pakistani soldiers and civilians, threatening Pakistan's security in a way that directly resulted from the Taliban's refusal to suppress their Pakistani brethren. This has fundamentally strained the previously close Pakistan-Taliban relationship.

laws.title: Wakhan Corridor Ecology
laws.subtitle: Remote Ecosystem and Wildlife Corridor
laws.fullDescription: The Wakhan Corridor — a narrow strip of Afghan territory connecting to China's Xinjiang — is one of Asia's most ecologically significant and least-disturbed areas. The corridor houses Marco Polo sheep (one of the world's largest sheep species), snow leopards, wolves, brown bears, and endangered Amur falcon populations. The Wakhan is home to the Wakhi and Kyrgyz peoples maintaining traditional pastoral nomadic lifestyles. Minimal road infrastructure has preserved the ecology. Under Taliban rule, international conservation NGOs have withdrawn but traditional community conservation norms remain. Climate change threatens Pamir glaciers that feed Wakhan valley water.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: poaching in remote areas: minimal enforcement capacity; traditional hunting by Wakhi and Kyrgyz communities: customary practice recognized
exceptions: Community-based conservation norms in Wakhan — particularly around Marco Polo sheep — provide traditional protection
Emergency conservation monitoring by satellite and remote sensing continues without in-country presence

quiz.q: What makes the Wakhan Corridor ecologically significant?
options: It contains Afghanistan's largest oil deposits
One of Asia's most ecologically significant and least-disturbed areas — housing Marco Polo sheep, snow leopards, and unique Pamir ecosystems
It is the site of the world's highest agricultural production
It is the only area in Afghanistan without land mine contamination
quiz.explanation: The Wakhan Corridor is one of Asia's most ecologically significant wilderness areas — a narrow strip of Afghan territory connecting to China, protected by its extreme remoteness and minimal road infrastructure. It houses Marco Polo sheep, snow leopards, brown bears, wolves, and unique Pamir ecosystems, while its indigenous Wakhi and Kyrgyz communities maintain traditional pastoral lifestyles that have coexisted with wildlife for millennia.

laws.title: Afghanistan's Long-Term Future
laws.subtitle: Pathways to Stability or Continued Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's long-term future involves several possible pathways: (1) Taliban entrenchment — continued harsh rule with international isolation, generating ongoing humanitarian crisis and instability; (2) Taliban moderation — internal pressure or international engagement gradually moderates Taliban policies, particularly on girls' education; (3) Taliban collapse — internal fractures (Kandahar vs. Kabul; Haqqani vs. Quetta Shura; moderates vs. hardliners) or ISKP pressure causes governance breakdown; (4) Negotiated settlement — regional and international actors engineer political transition including non-Taliban actors. Most analysts consider options 2-4 unlikely in the near term. International community faces agonizing choice between principled isolation and pragmatic engagement.
laws.penalty: No current enforcement mechanism for desired governance outcomes; long-term accountability possible through ICC for documented war crimes and crimes against humanity
exceptions: International engagement maintained at humanitarian level regardless of political non-recognition
UN Special Envoy process provides diplomatic channel for eventual political resolution

quiz.q: What internal Taliban division could affect Afghanistan's future stability?
options: Taliban are completely unified — no internal divisions
Kandahar (Akhundzada faction) vs. Kabul (Haqqani Network) tensions — along with moderates vs. hardliners on governance
Only tribal divisions among Taliban fighters
Taliban vs. former government members who joined the Taliban
quiz.explanation: Internal Taliban divisions — primarily between the Kandahar-based Akhundzada-led faction (hardline ideologues) and the Kabul-based Haqqani Network (pragmatic operators with Pakistan ties) — represent one of the key uncertainties in Afghanistan's future. These factions have different priorities, international relationships, and governance approaches. Escalating tensions could fracture Taliban governance, though external pressure has historically united the Taliban against common enemies.

laws.title: Afghan Diaspora and Remittances
laws.subtitle: USD Billions Supporting Families in Afghanistan
laws.fullDescription: The Afghan diaspora — estimated at 5-6 million people globally in countries including the US, Germany, Australia, UK, Canada, Iran, and Pakistan — sends hundreds of millions of dollars in remittances annually to family members in Afghanistan. These remittances are a critical lifeline — providing cash income in a collapsed formal economy. After the Taliban takeover, remittance flows initially increased dramatically as Afghans tried to support family members. Hawala operators transmit most remittances given the absence of formal banking. Western Union and money transfer services have partially restored Afghanistan operations. The diaspora also plays a political role — advocating for human rights in Afghan communities abroad.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: receiving remittances from diaspora: legal; converting foreign currency: Taliban-registered hawala operators only; sanctions: specific designated Taliban individuals cannot receive funds from sanctioned parties
exceptions: Humanitarian remittances for family survival are explicitly protected under OFAC and EU sanctions exceptions
Mobile money transfers operating through licensed Afghan telecoms operate with regulatory approval

quiz.q: How do most international remittances reach Afghans given the absence of formal banking?
options: Wire transfers through Western banks
Direct cash delivery by travelers
Hawala informal money transfer networks — the primary mechanism for remittances given collapsed banking
Cryptocurrency exclusively
quiz.explanation: The vast majority of international remittances reach Afghan families through hawala — the ancient trust-based informal money transfer network. With most international banks severing correspondent banking with Afghanistan due to sanctions risk, hawala operators transmit funds from Afghan diaspora worldwide to family members in Afghanistan. The system operates on trust between hawala operators, with no physical money crossing borders.

laws.title: Moral Police and Vice Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Ministry for Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban recreated the Ministry for Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) — known colloquially as the 'morality police' — identical to their first rule (1996-2001). PVPV enforcers patrol streets enforcing Taliban moral codes: women's dress and mahram requirements, men's beard length, prayer attendance, music prohibition, and other behavioral requirements. PVPV members carry whips and sticks. The PVPV has beaten men for short beards and women for showing ankles. Reports of PVPV members arresting individuals for phone screens showing music. The PVPV operates as a feared extrajudicial enforcement mechanism separate from the formal police.
laws.penalty: Violations of PVPV-enforced codes: immediate physical punishment (beating with whips/sticks), arrest; men without beards: beating and forced beard growing; women without mahram: arrest of woman and family; playing music: destruction of instruments
exceptions: Foreign nationals (diplomats, UN staff) are generally not subject to PVPV enforcement
Healthcare settings have some exemption from dress and mahram rules — female medical staff have limited protection

quiz.q: What is the PVPV and what role does it play under Taliban rule?
options: A humanitarian organization providing vaccines
The Ministry for Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice — morality police enforcing Taliban codes through street patrols and physical punishment
A political party advising the Taliban
A financial regulatory body
quiz.explanation: The PVPV (Ministry for Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice) is the Taliban's morality police — enforcers who patrol streets ensuring compliance with Taliban behavioral codes including women's dress, mahram requirements, men's beard length, prayer attendance, and music prohibition. PVPV members carry whips and sticks and administer immediate physical punishment. The PVPV was a defining feature of the first Taliban rule (1996-2001) and was immediately recreated after 2021.

laws.title: International Aid Architecture
laws.subtitle: USD 3+ Billion Annual Humanitarian Budget
laws.fullDescription: International humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan — channeled through UN agencies and NGOs to bypass the Taliban government — constitutes one of the world's largest annual humanitarian operations. In 2022-2023, the UN Humanitarian Response Plan for Afghanistan sought USD 4+ billion annually. This massive aid flow maintains basic survival for tens of millions of Afghans. The architecture involves: OCHA coordinating overall response; WFP for food; UNICEF for children; WHO for health; UNHCR for refugees; hundreds of NGO implementing partners. Donor fatigue in 2023-2024 has reduced funding — with severe consequences for program delivery and Afghan survival.
laws.penalty: Aid diversion by Taliban: criminal prosecution in donor countries; NGO compliance violations with Taliban restrictions: program suspension; humanitarian workers: face risk of Taliban detention
exceptions: OFAC and EU sanctions contain explicit humanitarian exceptions allowing all essential aid transactions
UN agencies operate under UNSC authorization providing some protection from Taliban interference

quiz.q: Why is international aid channeled through UN agencies and NGOs rather than the Afghan government?
options: UN agencies are more efficient than governments
The Afghan government requested it for capacity reasons
To bypass the Taliban government — preventing aid from legitimizing Taliban rule while ensuring delivery to the population
It is required under WTO international trade rules
quiz.explanation: International aid is channeled through UN agencies and NGOs specifically to bypass the Taliban government — avoiding the political problem of directly funding a government whose human rights record, terrorism connections, and lack of legitimacy make direct aid impossible. This creates a parallel governance system where UN/NGO 'humanitarian systems' deliver essential services that a legitimate government would provide, without providing the Taliban with resources or legitimacy.

laws.title: Afghan National Army Collapse
laws.subtitle: 300,000 Troops to Zero in Days
laws.fullDescription: The Afghan National Army (ANA) — built at a cost of over USD 88 billion by the US and NATO over 20 years, equipped with modern weapons, aircraft, and trained by Western advisors — collapsed in days in August 2021 as Taliban forces advanced. Analysts cite: corruption draining troop numbers (ghost soldiers on payrolls), dependence on US air support that evaporated, demoralized troops unwilling to fight for an unpopular government, and Taliban infiltration. Billions in US military equipment — aircraft, vehicles, weapons — fell into Taliban hands. The collapse shocked Western capitals and represented one of the most rapid military defeats in modern history.
laws.penalty: Former ANA members: face Taliban reprisals despite amnesty promises — documented extrajudicial killings; serving Taliban: former ANA members who joined Taliban operate under Taliban military law
exceptions: Some former ANA members fled to join National Resistance Front in Panjshir
Former special forces members who managed to evacuate provide intelligence and training support to Afghan diaspora resistance efforts
laws.sourceLabel: SIGAR — US Inspector General for Afghanistan

quiz.q: How much did the US spend building the Afghan National Army that collapsed in days?
options: USD 10 billion
USD 40 billion
Over USD 88 billion — making it one of history's most expensive and failed military investments
USD 200 billion
