quiz.explanation: The US spent over USD 88 billion building, equipping, training, and sustaining the Afghan National Army over 20 years — one of the largest foreign military assistance programs in history. When the US completed its withdrawal in August 2021, this force of nominally 300,000 troops collapsed within days, surrendering to Taliban without meaningful resistance in most provinces. Billions in modern military equipment fell into Taliban hands.

laws.title: Timber Trade and Forest Loss
laws.subtitle: Cedar and Oak Forests of Nuristan
laws.fullDescription: Nuristan and Kunar provinces in eastern Afghanistan contain some of the country's last significant forests — including cedar (deodar), oak, and pine. These forests have been commercially logged for decades, with timber smuggled to Pakistan via border mountain routes. During the 2001-2021 period, international conservation organizations worked to reduce illegal logging, but limited governance and corruption prevented effective enforcement. Under Taliban rule, logging continues — with Taliban taxing or directly participating in timber trade. FAO estimates Afghanistan has lost over 60% of its forest cover since 1978. Forest loss accelerates erosion, reduces water retention, and destroys biodiversity.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: unauthorized logging outside Taliban-sanctioned operations: fines and corporal punishment; commercial timber export: requires Taliban authorization with tax payment; forest arson: severe punishment
exceptions: Subsistence fuel wood collection by local communities: generally tolerated as survival necessity
FAO reforestation programs operate under humanitarian authorization

quiz.q: Which Afghan provinces contain the country's remaining significant forests?
options: Helmand and Kandahar provinces
Kabul and Logar provinces
Nuristan and Kunar provinces in eastern Afghanistan — with cedar, oak, and pine forests
Herat and Farah provinces
quiz.explanation: Nuristan and Kunar provinces in eastern Afghanistan contain the country's remaining significant forest cover — including deodar cedar, oak, and pine. These mountainous eastern provinces border Pakistan and have seen centuries of timber trade. Afghanistan has lost over 60% of its original forest cover since 1978, with illegal logging a persistent problem. Remaining forests are critical for watershed protection and biodiversity but face ongoing pressure.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Under Taliban
laws.subtitle: Taliban Corruption vs. Previous Government
laws.fullDescription: Ironically, Taliban governance has reduced some forms of corruption endemic under the previous government — particularly police checkpoint bribery and bureaucratic corruption. The Taliban's ideological discipline and fear-based enforcement has reduced shakedowns of ordinary Afghans. However, Taliban governance creates new corruption forms: commanders extorting businesses, nepotism in appointments, diversion of humanitarian aid, and use of confiscated properties for personal enrichment. The Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index historically ranked Afghanistan near the bottom globally. Taliban governance substitutes ideological enforcement for anti-corruption mechanisms.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: corruption by ordinary officials: severe corporal punishment including lashing documented; senior Taliban corruption: effectively immune from accountability; bribery of Taliban: complex — some commanders actively solicit
exceptions: Taliban Supreme Court has jurisdiction over corruption — but senior Taliban are functionally immune
Tribal and community dispute mechanisms provide accountability for low-level official corruption in some areas

quiz.q: How has corruption changed under Taliban rule compared to the previous government?
options: Corruption has been completely eliminated
Corruption has dramatically increased at all levels
Some forms of petty corruption reduced (police shakedowns) but new Taliban-specific corruption emerged (commander extortion, property seizures)
Corruption is identical to the previous government
quiz.explanation: Taliban governance has created a mixed corruption picture: some forms of petty corruption endemic under the previous government (police checkpoint bribery, bureaucratic shakedowns) have reduced due to Taliban ideological discipline and fear. However, new Taliban-specific corruption has emerged: commanders extorting businesses, nepotism in Taliban appointments, diversion of humanitarian aid, and appropriation of confiscated properties for personal benefit.

laws.title: Polio Eradication Challenges
laws.subtitle: WHO and Afghanistan's Last Poliovirus Stronghold
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan and Pakistan are the world's only two countries where polio has never been eradicated — making them the last global reservoirs of wild poliovirus. The Taliban restricted vaccination campaigns during their insurgency (2001-2021) — leading to polio worker killings and campaign disruptions. Under Taliban governance, there have been efforts to cooperate with WHO polio campaigns — recognizing the religious acceptability of the vaccination. Taliban have generally allowed national immunization days. However, security incidents (ISKP attacks on health workers), access restrictions, and nomadic population challenges make eradication extremely difficult.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: obstructing WHO polio vaccination: not currently Taliban policy — cooperation generally maintained; vaccine refusal by parents: no criminal penalty but social health pressure
exceptions: WHO emergency health programs including polio vaccination operate under negotiated Taliban access
Islamic religious authorities have issued fatwas (religious rulings) supporting polio vaccination — addressing religious objections

quiz.q: Why are Afghanistan and Pakistan the world's only remaining wild poliovirus reservoirs?
options: They have insufficient vaccine supply
Religious objections make vaccination impossible
Combined factors: insurgency disrupting campaigns, security incidents targeting health workers, nomadic population movement, and cross-border transmission
Government policy prohibits international vaccination
quiz.explanation: Afghanistan and Pakistan remain the world's only wild poliovirus reservoirs due to a combination of factors: decades of insurgency disrupting vaccination campaigns, targeted killings of polio health workers by extremists (wrongly suspecting vaccination as espionage), nomadic populations crossing the border carrying virus, and cross-border transmission between the two countries. Despite significant progress, eradication remains elusive due to these compounding challenges.

laws.title: Ministry System Under Taliban
laws.subtitle: Governance Structure Without Technocrats
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban govern through a ministerial system in Kabul — with ministries for Interior, Defense, Foreign Affairs, Education, Health, Finance, and others. However, most technocratic expertise has fled — doctors, engineers, economists, and administrators have largely evacuated. Ministries are staffed primarily by Taliban loyalists with religious education but limited technical expertise. The Finance Ministry has maintained some function — collecting customs revenue. The Health Ministry struggles without female healthcare workers. The Education Ministry oversees the madrassa expansion while girls' education is banned. Governance quality is extremely limited across all ministries.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: operating programs without ministerial authorization: confiscation and arrest; NGOs and UN agencies require ministerial agreements to operate
exceptions: UN agencies have framework agreements with Taliban ministries establishing operational parameters
Emergency operations during disasters may proceed with expedited ministerial authorization

quiz.q: What challenge does the Taliban government face in ministerial governance?
options: Too many qualified technocrats competing for positions
Ministries are well-staffed with qualified professionals
Most technical expertise (doctors, engineers, economists) fled Afghanistan — leaving ministries staffed by religiously trained Taliban loyalists with limited technical skills
International organizations refuse to interact with any Taliban ministries
quiz.explanation: Taliban ministries face a severe human capital deficit: most Afghan technocrats — doctors, engineers, economists, administrators, lawyers — fled Afghanistan after the 2021 takeover, depriving ministries of essential expertise. What remains are predominantly Taliban loyalists with religious education but limited technical governance skills. This 'brain drain' severely limits the Taliban's ability to govern even the functions they wish to maintain.

laws.title: Informal Economy and Street Markets
laws.subtitle: Kabul Bazaar Under Taliban Rule
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan's formal economy has largely collapsed, but an extensive informal economy operates — particularly in urban bazaars (markets). Kabul's major bazaars (Mandawi, Chicken Street, Karte Seh) continue trading. Street vendors, food markets, and small-scale traders function. The informal economy operates largely without registration, taxation (beyond Taliban checkpoints), or legal protection. Women are largely excluded from market trading under Taliban restrictions. The informal economy includes considerable smuggling — goods moving across porous borders. Remittances and humanitarian cash injections fuel consumption in informal markets.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: trading without Taliban checkpoint fee payment: confiscation; women trading without mahram: punishment; selling prohibited goods (music, Western content): criminal prosecution
exceptions: Food and essential goods markets operate with minimal Taliban interference beyond checkpoint fees
Emergency cash distribution by humanitarian organizations fuels informal market spending — tolerated as economic stabilizer

quiz.q: How has Afghanistan's economic activity survived despite formal economic collapse?
options: The formal economy has fully recovered
Only foreign aid sustains any economic activity
An extensive informal bazaar economy persists — fueled by remittances and humanitarian cash injections
The Taliban created a new formal economic system
quiz.explanation: Despite the collapse of the formal economy, Afghanistan's traditional bazaar (market) culture provides economic continuity. Informal markets in Kabul and provincial cities trade food, goods, and services outside formal regulation — beyond Taliban checkpoint fees. This informal economy is fueled by diaspora remittances and humanitarian cash assistance, providing subsistence economic activity while the formal banking and business sector remains largely non-functional.

laws.title: Taliban-al-Qaeda Historical Relationship
laws.subtitle: Ideological and Personal Ties
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban and al-Qaeda share a 30-year relationship — personal, ideological, and operational. Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda established Afghan training camps in the 1990s with Taliban permission. The Taliban refused to extradite bin Laden after 9/11 — leading to the US-led intervention. Many al-Qaeda leaders married into Afghan tribal families connected to Taliban leaders — creating kinship ties that transcend organizational distinctions. The Doha Agreement (2020) committed Taliban to break from al-Qaeda; al-Zawahiri's 2022 Kabul killing demonstrates this commitment was hollow. Al-Qaeda's global ambitions and Taliban's primarily Afghan focus create some divergence of interests, but ties remain deep.
laws.penalty: Under international law: Taliban harboring al-Qaeda: potential use of force justification under UNSC Resolution 1373; sanctions: UNSC al-Qaeda sanctions list covers key individuals
exceptions: Taliban distinguish between al-Qaeda's global jihad agenda (which they nominally disavow) and personal/family ties (which they maintain)
US counter-terrorism operations continue targeting al-Qaeda in Afghanistan under AUMF (Authorization for Use of Military Force) legal framework

quiz.q: What personal ties link Taliban and al-Qaeda leaders beyond organizational affiliation?
options: Only financial ties — al-Qaeda paid Taliban for safe haven
Taliban and al-Qaeda have no personal connections
Marriage ties between al-Qaeda leaders and Afghan tribal families connected to Taliban — creating kinship that transcends organizational distinctions
They share only religious education backgrounds
quiz.explanation: Taliban-al-Qaeda ties extend beyond organizational affiliation to include kinship bonds — al-Qaeda leaders including Osama bin Laden and others arranged marriages into Afghan tribal families with Taliban connections. In Pashtun culture, these kinship ties create obligations of loyalty and hospitality that are extraordinarily difficult to break. These personal bonds explain why Taliban have consistently failed to truly sever ties with al-Qaeda despite international pressure and formal commitments.

laws.title: Punishment for Blasphemy
laws.subtitle: Taliban Sharia Enforcement for Religious Offenses
laws.fullDescription: Under Taliban's interpretation of Sharia, blasphemy — insulting Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, or Islamic doctrine — is punishable by death. Afghanistan under Taliban has applied this to both Muslims (apostasy) and non-Muslims (blasphemy). Social media posts critical of Islamic doctrine or positive about non-Islamic religion can lead to death sentences. The Taliban have conducted executions and imprisonment for religious offenses. This extends to criticism of Taliban governance framed as 'un-Islamic' — allowing the Taliban to use blasphemy charges as a political enforcement tool against critics.
laws.penalty: Blasphemy: death penalty under Taliban's Sharia interpretation; apostasy: death; criticizing Islamic doctrine: imprisonment or execution; 'un-Islamic' social media: arrest and potential death penalty
exceptions: Foreign non-Muslims (diplomats, aid workers) have some practical protection from blasphemy prosecution — though not formal legal immunity
Taliban have used blasphemy charges selectively — primarily targeting Afghan critics and civil society rather than applying uniformly

quiz.q: How do Taliban use blasphemy laws as a political tool?
options: They only apply blasphemy laws to actual religious offenses with no political dimension
Blasphemy charges are only used against non-Muslims
Blasphemy charges are applied to critics by framing criticism of Taliban governance as 'un-Islamic' — a political enforcement mechanism
Taliban do not enforce blasphemy laws — only religious courts do
quiz.explanation: The Taliban use blasphemy charges as a political enforcement tool — framing criticism of Taliban governance as 'un-Islamic' and therefore blasphemous. This creates a powerful censorship mechanism: any criticism of Taliban policy can be reframed as an attack on Islamic governance, making it a capital offense. This conflation of political criticism with religious offense is a classic feature of theocratic governance.

laws.title: Wetlands and Migratory Birds
laws.subtitle: Ab-i-Estada and Hamoun Wetlands
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan hosts several critical wetland ecosystems important for Central Asian migratory birds. Ab-i-Estada lake (Ghazni province) is a RAMSAR-listed wetland hosting hundreds of thousands of flamingos and migratory waterfowl. The Hamoun wetlands (shared with Iran) support extraordinary biodiversity when water levels are adequate — but have largely dried due to Helmand River water reductions. Under Taliban rule, RAMSAR obligations are formally unrecognized — no environmental governance exists. Bird hunting (including of protected species) for food and commercial trade has increased without enforcement. Climate change threatens all Afghan wetlands.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: protected species hunting: no formal prohibition or enforcement; wetland drainage for agriculture: minimal enforcement; illegal wildlife trade: informal market sanctions only
exceptions: RAMSAR International maintains diplomatic engagement for wetland conservation — though Taliban governance provides no practical protection
Migratory bird treaties involve international legal obligations that the IEA neither recognizes nor enforces

quiz.q: What remarkable wildlife congregation occurs at Ab-i-Estada wetland in Afghanistan?
options: Thousands of snow leopards gather for mating season
Hundreds of thousands of flamingos and migratory waterfowl — a critically important Central Asian staging area
The world's largest crane migration
Brown bear populations gather for spawning salmon
quiz.explanation: Ab-i-Estada lake in Ghazni province hosts hundreds of thousands of flamingos and migratory waterfowl — one of Central Asia's most important bird staging and breeding areas. The lake is a RAMSAR-listed wetland of international importance. Under Taliban governance, this extraordinary wildlife resource has no formal protection — hunting pressure has increased and international conservation monitoring has largely ceased.

laws.title: Maternal Mortality Crisis
laws.subtitle: One of World's Highest Maternal Death Rates
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has one of the world's highest maternal mortality rates — estimated at 620 deaths per 100,000 live births (global average: 211; wealthy countries: under 10). Under Taliban rule, female healthcare workers have been restricted, many have fled, and hospitals lack supplies. Women must have a mahram (male guardian) to access healthcare — creating barriers when family members are unavailable. Female obstetricians and gynecologists have largely been removed from practice or fled. UNICEF and WHO document rapidly worsening maternal health indicators. Skilled birth attendance — critical for reducing maternal mortality — has declined sharply.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: women accessing healthcare without mahram: risk of punishment depending on province; male doctors treating female patients: restrictions in some areas; NGO maternal health programs: operating under negotiated Taliban access
exceptions: Healthcare emergency exception: some areas allow emergency obstetric care without strict mahram requirements
International NGO maternal health clinics maintain operations under humanitarian framework agreements

quiz.q: What barrier does the mahram requirement create for Afghan women accessing healthcare?
options: No barrier — mahram requirement only applies to travel, not healthcare
Women can access healthcare freely regardless of Taliban rules
Women must have a male guardian present for healthcare — creating barriers when male family members are unavailable or when only female providers are culturally acceptable
Mahram requirement applies only to mental health services
quiz.explanation: The Taliban's mahram requirement — mandating a male guardian accompanies women outside the home — creates significant barriers to healthcare access. When male family members are unavailable (working, deceased, away), women cannot access care. Additionally, many Afghan women only accept care from female providers, and with female doctors largely removed, the intersection of mahram requirements and female provider absence creates compounded healthcare access barriers.

laws.title: Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining
laws.subtitle: Lapis Lazuli, Emeralds, and Gemstone Trade
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan has extraordinary gemstone resources — the world's finest lapis lazuli (from Badakhshan, traded for 6,000 years), high-quality emeralds (Panjshir Valley, Kunar), rubies (Jegdalek), tourmalines, and other precious stones. Artisanal small-scale mining is a traditional livelihood for thousands of Afghan miners. The Taliban tax and regulate artisanal gemstone mining — a significant revenue source. Afghan lapis lazuli appears in luxury goods globally; Panjshir emeralds are sold in Dubai and international gem markets. Smuggling is extensive — gems move through Pakistan and Dubai channels avoiding formal taxation.
laws.penalty: Under Taliban: unauthorized gemstone mining: confiscation and imprisonment; gem smuggling: criminal prosecution and confiscation; failure to pay Taliban mining tax: violent enforcement documented
exceptions: Traditional community mining rights recognized with Taliban tax payment replacing previous government licensing
Emergency mining for survival in remote areas treated with some tolerance — subsistence exception
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Mines and Petroleum Afghanistan

quiz.q: For how many years has Afghan lapis lazuli been traded globally?
options: About 500 years
Around 1,000 years
Approximately 6,000 years — one of the world's oldest international trade goods
Only since the 19th century
quiz.explanation: Afghan lapis lazuli — sourced from Badakhshan province — has been traded internationally for approximately 6,000 years, making it one of the world's oldest traded commodities. Ancient Egyptian artifacts, including the burial mask of Tutankhamun, contain lapis lazuli from Afghan mines. Today, Badakhshan remains the world's primary source of fine lapis lazuli — a trade route stretching back to the Bronze Age that continues under Taliban governance.

laws.title: Taliban Supreme Leader Authority
laws.subtitle: Theocratic Command and Control
laws.fullDescription: Taliban governance is structured as a theocracy with Haibatullah Akhundzada as Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful) — a title claiming religious authority over all Muslims, not just Afghans. His decrees are treated as divine command requiring no parliamentary or legal process. Akhundzada is rarely seen publicly — governing from Kandahar through written decrees. The Rahbari Shura (Leadership Council) advises but does not constrain. There are no elections, no legislative body, no separation of powers, and no judicial independence. This concentration of unchecked authority in one figure is unique globally and creates extreme governance fragility — everything depends on one opaque leader.
laws.penalty: Disobeying Taliban Supreme Leader's decree: treated as religious sin and criminal offense — punishment up to execution; questioning Taliban authority structure: arrest and torture
exceptions: Tribal leaders in some areas have some latitude in implementation — distance from Kandahar creating de facto regional autonomy
International interlocutors communicate with Kabul-based Taliban officials who have some policy flexibility within limits set by Kandahar

quiz.q: What does the title 'Amir al-Mu'minin' claimed by Taliban leader Akhundzada mean?
options: President of the Islamic Republic
Commander of the Faithful — a title claiming religious authority over all Muslims
Prime Minister of the Taliban government
Supreme Judge of Islamic Law
quiz.explanation: 'Amir al-Mu'minin' (Commander of the Faithful) is the title claimed by Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada — historically used by the Caliph of all Muslims. By claiming this title, the Taliban assert not just political authority over Afghanistan but religious authority over the global Muslim community. This claim has been rejected by virtually all Muslim-majority countries and Islamic scholars, but within Afghanistan it provides the ideological foundation for absolute unchecked authority.

laws.title: Women and Technology Access
laws.subtitle: Mobile Phones and Digital Restrictions
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have issued decrees restricting women's use of mobile phones and internet. In some provinces, women are prohibited from using smartphones without a mahram's permission. Taliban fighters have stopped women on streets and checked their phones — arresting those with 'un-Islamic' content. The digital restriction creates particular hardship: women cannot seek employment, education, healthcare information, or contact family abroad. Underground networks of Afghan women use encrypted apps (WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram) to maintain communication and support networks despite risks. The digital gender gap in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan is extreme.
laws.penalty: Women using mobile phones with prohibited content: confiscation and arrest; 'un-Islamic' app content on phones: destruction of device and potential arrest; women operating social media accounts: documentation of violation and prosecution
exceptions: Women using phones for approved purposes (family communication, healthcare emergencies) in some areas tolerated
Female doctors and healthcare workers may use phones for work with authorization in some provinces

quiz.q: What digital restriction has the Taliban imposed on women in some provinces?
options: Women are prohibited from owning any electronic device
Women are prohibited from using smartphones without a mahram's permission — with phone checks conducted by Taliban fighters
Women may use phones only for calling — no internet
Women may only access Taliban-approved websites
quiz.explanation: In some Taliban-controlled provinces, women are prohibited from using smartphones without their mahram's (male guardian's) permission. Taliban fighters have stopped women to check their phones, arresting those with content deemed un-Islamic. This digital restriction compounds women's isolation — preventing them from accessing information, employment, education, healthcare guidance, or maintaining contact with family abroad. Underground networks use encrypted apps despite these risks.

laws.title: Execution Methods and Public Punishment
laws.subtitle: Taliban Judicial Killings and Spectacle
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have conducted public executions — primarily shootings — in soccer stadiums and public spaces. Executions are carried out for murder (unless blood money paid), apostasy, adultery, and terrorism (ISKP membership). In some cases, bodies have been publicly displayed. Amputation — for theft — has been publicly conducted. The Taliban use public punishment as a tool of social control and demonstration of authority. International human rights organizations document these executions; the UN has called them violations of minimum due process standards. The spectacle of public punishment was a defining feature of the first Taliban rule and has returned.
laws.penalty: Murder (qisas): execution or blood money (diya) paid to family; apostasy: death; adultery: stoning; theft: amputation; terrorism: execution; drug trafficking (major): execution
exceptions: Blood money (diya) payment to victim's family prevents qisas (execution) in murder cases — allowing financial resolution
Juvenile offenders subject to modified sentences — though minimum age standards not clearly defined or consistently applied

quiz.q: Where have Taliban conducted public executions and amputations?
options: Only in remote areas — away from public view
In secret detention facilities exclusively
In soccer stadiums and public spaces — public punishment as a social control tool
Only in the Supreme Court building
quiz.explanation: The Taliban have conducted public executions and amputations in soccer stadiums and other public spaces — deliberately making punishment a public spectacle. This mirrors their first period of rule (1996-2001) when the Kabul soccer stadium was a regular execution venue. UN human rights monitors have documented these executions, noting the absence of minimum due process standards. The public nature of punishment is intentional — serving as a deterrent and demonstration of Taliban authority.

laws.title: Water Law and Transboundary Rivers
laws.subtitle: Amu Darya and Regional Water Governance
laws.fullDescription: Afghanistan shares major river systems with neighbors — the Amu Darya (with Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan), Helmand (with Iran), Kabul River (flowing into Pakistan), and others. There is no comprehensive transboundary water governance framework. Soviet-era bilateral water agreements govern some Amu Darya allocation. Climate change is reducing overall water availability in the region while population growth increases demand. Upstream Afghanistan has legal rights under international water law to use water for development — but downstream countries (Iran, Uzbekistan) depend on flows. The Taliban have shown interest in hydropower development but lack technical and financial capacity.
laws.penalty: Under IEA: unilateral diversion of transboundary rivers: potential international dispute; domestic water theft from shared systems: tribal dispute resolution; dam construction without downstream notification: violation of international water law principles
exceptions: Customary international water law principles of 'equitable utilization' provide framework — though IEA doesn't formally accept international law
Humanitarian water access exempt from normal water allocation negotiations

quiz.q: Which major river is shared between Afghanistan and multiple Central Asian countries?
options: The Nile
The Mekong
The Amu Darya (Oxus) — shared with Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan
The Indus
quiz.explanation: The Amu Darya (historically the Oxus River) originates in the Pamir Mountains and forms Afghanistan's northern border — shared with Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. It is the region's most important river, feeding the Aral Sea basin and providing water for millions across Central Asia. Climate change reducing glacial meltwater in the Pamirs threatens the long-term water supply of all riparian states.

laws.title: Music and Arts Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Cultural Genocide and Heritage Destruction
laws.fullDescription: The Taliban have banned music — one of their defining cultural prohibitions applied during both their first rule (1996-2001) and again after 2021. Afghan classical music (including the rubab lute tradition), traditional folk songs, wedding music, and radio broadcasting of music are all prohibited. Musicians have fled Afghanistan; instruments have been burned. The Afghan National Institute of Music — internationally acclaimed — relocated to Portugal. Films, TV dramas, and visual arts depicting living beings are banned or severely restricted. Cultural heritage sites receive minimal protection. The UN describes Taliban cultural restrictions as threatening intangible cultural heritage.
laws.penalty: Playing musical instruments: destruction of instruments and beating/imprisonment of musicians; broadcasting music: criminal prosecution; organizing musical events: arrest; possessing music on phone: punishment
exceptions: Nasheed (Islamic vocal music without instruments) is permitted — a narrow exception maintaining some musical tradition
Afghan cultural diaspora communities preserve music and arts freely outside Afghanistan

quiz.q: What happened to the Afghan National Institute of Music under Taliban rule?
options: It continues operating with reduced programming
Taliban took it over and converted it to a madrassa
It relocated to Portugal — after Taliban banned music and threatened its students and faculty
It was burned down by Taliban forces
quiz.explanation: The Afghan National Institute of Music — internationally acclaimed for educating Afghan musicians including the all-female Zohra Orchestra — relocated to Portugal after the Taliban's return. Unable to operate in Taliban Afghanistan where music is banned, the institute sought refuge in Europe to continue its mission of preserving Afghan musical heritage. Its internationally celebrated all-female orchestra became a symbol of Afghan cultural achievement that Taliban rule effectively exiled.

laws.title: Afghanistan's Place in International Law
laws.subtitle: State Continuity, Treaties, and IEA Obligations
laws.fullDescription: Under international law, Afghanistan as a state continues to exist and is bound by its previous treaty obligations — even though the government has changed. This means: UN Charter obligations; Geneva Convention protections for civilians in armed conflict; Convention on the Rights of the Child; Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW); international environmental agreements. The IEA does not recognize these obligations but cannot escape them under state continuity doctrine. This creates a unique legal situation: Afghanistan is simultaneously bound by international law it rejects, governed by a regime that claims Sharia supersedes international law, and monitored by international bodies that have lost effective access.
laws.penalty: Under international law: Afghanistan remains bound by all previous treaty obligations regardless of government change; practical enforcement depends on bilateral relationships and multilateral mechanisms
exceptions: Customary international law obligations (jus cogens norms) — prohibition on genocide, slavery, torture — bind all states regardless of treaty ratification
ICC universal jurisdiction provides potential accountability framework independent of Afghan government consent

quiz.q: Under international law, is Afghanistan still bound by treaties signed by the previous government?
options: No — when a government changes, all previous treaties are void
Only treaties ratified before 1990 remain valid
Yes — under state continuity doctrine, Afghanistan remains bound by all previous treaty obligations despite the government change
Only bilateral treaties remain — multilateral treaties require re-ratification
quiz.explanation: Under the international law principle of state continuity, Afghanistan as a state remains bound by all treaty obligations undertaken by previous governments — including the UN Charter, Geneva Conventions, CEDAW, Convention on the Rights of the Child, and hundreds of other international agreements. The IEA cannot unilaterally renounce these obligations simply by changing the government. This creates a legal framework for holding Afghanistan accountable even though the IEA rejects international law in favor of Sharia.
